Clinical Reference

Bradyarrhythmia & Heart Block

On this page
A heart rate too slow to meet the body's demand — either the sinus node stops firing (sinus node dysfunction) or the impulse stops arriving (AV block). The rate number matters far less than two things: are they symptomatic, and where is the block.
Bradycardia = HR <50/min Narrow QRS = nodal · Wide QRS = infranodal Mobitz II / high-grade / CHB → pacing Atropine 1 mg IV q3–5 min, max 3 mg No pill treats bradycardia — the therapy is a pacemaker
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story

The heart has no external clock. It builds its own beat from a chain of cells that leak themselves to threshold, and then hands that beat down a wiring tree to the muscle. Bradycardia means one of exactly two things has gone wrong, and separating them is the first move at every bedside:

  • The generator failed — the sinus node isn't firing often enough, or its output can't escape into the atrium. That is sinus node dysfunction (SND). On the ECG, P waves are missing.
  • The wire failed — the sinus node fires perfectly well, but the impulse doesn't reach the ventricle. That is AV block. On the ECG, P waves are present but not followed by a QRS.

That single distinction — missing P waves vs blocked P waves — sorts nearly every bradycardia you will ever see, and it costs you one glance at a rhythm strip.

Think of the conduction system as a train line. The SA node is the dispatcher who decides when a train leaves. The AV node is a single-track section with a deliberate speed limit — it slows every train down on purpose, so the platform (the ventricle) has time to clear before the next arrives. The His-Purkinje system is the express track past that point: fast, and with no speed limit at all. Now the two failures read differently. No trains leaving = sinus node dysfunction. Trains leaving on schedule but not arriving = AV block. And where on the line the train stops decides everything: a train stuck in the slow single-track section (AV node) will still get through eventually, and there's a backup engine just past it. A train that dies on the express track (infranodal) is stranded in the middle of nowhere — the only backup is a slow, unreliable local engine that may not start at all.

The conduction chain, the two ways it fails, and why the level of failure — not the heart rate — is the prognosis.
The anatomy behind every rhythm strip: SA node → internodal tracts → AV node → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers.
Image: OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons
Where each structure lives on the tracing. P = atrium (SA node fired and captured). PR = mostly AV nodal delay. QRS = His-Purkinje + ventricle. Bradycardia is read by asking which of these is missing.
Image: Agateller (Anthony Atkielski), public domain — Wikimedia Commons

1 · Why the sinus node beats at all — the funny current

A working myocyte sits at a stable −90 mV and waits to be told what to do. A sinus nodal cell cannot sit still. After each beat it drifts upward from its maximum diastolic potential (≈ −60 mV) until it hits threshold (≈ −40 mV) and fires again. That upward drift is phase 4 diastolic depolarization, and its steepness is the heart rate. Flatten the slope and the rate falls; steepen it and the rate rises. Everything on your bradycardia algorithm is an attempt to bend this one line.

The drift is driven substantially by If — the "funny current," a mixed Na⁺/K⁺ inward current carried by HCN4 channels. It earned the name because it behaves backwards for a voltage-gated channel: it opens on hyperpolarization. So the more the cell repolarizes at the end of a beat, the more If turns on, and the harder it pulls the cell back up toward the next one. It is a self-restarting engine.

If is not the whole story, and modern reviews are careful here. Phase 4 is generated by a coupled-clock system: the "membrane clock" (If and friends) plus a "Ca²⁺ clock" — rhythmic SR calcium release that drives inward current through the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger late in diastole (Lakatta, Circ Res 2010). Say If initiates and contributes to the slope — the relative weighting of the two clocks is still openly debated by the people who discovered them.

This is not academic. Loss-of-function HCN4 mutations cause familial sinus bradycardia in humans — and the mechanism is beautiful: the mutant channel activates at more negative voltages, which, as the authors put it, "mimic those of mild vagal stimulation" (Milanesi, NEJM 2006). Knock HCN4 out of an adult mouse heart and you get If down ~70%, deep bradycardia, and progressive AV block — 1st degree → 2:1 → complete (Baruscotti, PNAS 2011). One channel, both halves of this guide.

Pacemaker phase-4 depolarization and its autonomic modulation — the target of every chronotrope you will push.

2 · The two knobs: vagal and sympathetic

Two opposing cascades converge on that slope, and knowing them means you never have to memorize a drug list.

LimbThe cascade, step by stepNet effectDrugs that live here
Vagal
(the brake)		 ACh → M₂ receptor → Gi → inhibits adenylyl cyclase → ↓cAMP → less If → flatter slope.
And in parallel, the freed Gβγ subunit binds and opens IKACh (GIRK1/GIRK4) directly → K⁺ efflux → hyperpolarization → the cell starts its climb from further away.		 ↓ SA rate
↓ AV nodal conduction (longer PR / AH)		 Atropine blocks M₂ — it doesn't stimulate the node, it releases this brake.
Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, pyridostigmine, neostigmine) push it harder.
Sympathetic
(the accelerator)		 NE/epi → β₁ → Gs → adenylyl cyclase → ↑cAMP. cAMP then does two things: binds HCN4 directly at its cyclic-nucleotide-binding domain (no phosphorylation needed) shifting activation to more positive voltages → steeper slope; and activates PKA → phosphorylates L-type Ca²⁺ channels → ↑ICaL. ↑ SA rate
↑ AV nodal conduction		 Epinephrine, dopamine, isoproterenol, dobutamine all agonize β₁.
β-blockers remove this — see the note below.
β-blockers do not block calcium channels. They remove the cAMP/PKA-mediated augmentation of ICaL and If. That makes their nodal effect sympathetic-tone-dependent — which is exactly why they bite hardest in a catecholamine-driven patient and underperform on a quiet or denervated node. The distinction is not pedantry: it predicts behavior.
The SA node desensitizes to sustained vagal stimulation; the AV node does not (Loeb, Am J Physiol 1981). That asymmetry explains a bedside puzzle: during a prolonged vagal surge the sinus rate creeps back up while the AV block stubbornly persists.

3 · Why the level of block is the whole ballgame

Two tissues, two different ion channels, two different personalities:

  • The compact AV node depolarizes predominantly through slow L-type Ca²⁺ channels, with sparse Nav1.5. Its upstroke is lazy (dV/dtmax ~4–6 V/s). It conducts decrementally — push it harder and it conducts worse, which is a feature, not a bug: it is the reason a patient in AF at 400 atrial beats/min doesn't fibrillate their ventricle.
  • The His-Purkinje system depolarizes through fast Na⁺ channels (Nav1.5), like working myocardium. It is built for speed, conducts all-or-none, and when it fails it fails suddenly.
Say it as a preference, not a partitionThis tissue split is the engine behind the whole guide, but the real biology is a gradient. The compact node and central SA node are Ca²⁺-dominant with sparse-to-absent Nav1.5; the transitional (AN/NH) zones and the nodal periphery are mixed. Likewise, flecainide "preferentially" hits fast-Na tissue but can also slow AV nodal conduction. Write and think "preferentially" — never "exclusively."

Now the payoff. Because the AV node is Ca²⁺-dependent and richly modulated by vagal tone, it is the tissue that β-blockers, diltiazem/verapamil, and digoxin act on, and the tissue atropine can rescue. Because the His-Purkinje system runs on fast Na⁺ channels, it is the tissue that class Ic agents and hyperkalemia poison — and the tissue atropine cannot help.

Hyperkalemia is functionally a sodium-channel blocker. Raising extracellular K⁺ depolarizes the resting membrane (−90 → −80 → as far as ≈ −60 mV). Because the rate of rise of phase 0 is proportional to the membrane potential at its onset, a depolarized cell has fewer available Na⁺ channels → ↓Vmax → slowed conduction → a wider and wider QRS, which eventually fuses with the T wave into the classic sine wave. It converges on the exact same final pathway as flecainide, from a completely different direction — which is why "check the potassium" is the cheapest thing you will do all night.
Why the level of block — not the heart rate — decides how scared to be.

4 · Why atropine fails — and can backfire — below the node

The usual explanation ("the His-Purkinje isn't vagally innervated") is not true, and you should stop saying it. Primary anatomic work found "a great abundance of cholinergic nerve endings in association with the ventricular conducting system" (Rardon & Bailey, JACC 1983), and studies using specific cholinergic markers find nerve fibres abundant in the His bundle and bundle branches. The clinical rule is rock-solid; the popular mechanism for it is folklore. Two better reasons actually explain it:

  • Why atropine doesn't help: infranodal block is structural — fibrosis, necrosis, infiltration — not vagally-maintained tone. An antimuscarinic has nothing to reverse. You cannot un-block scar by blocking a receptor. (Functionally, this tracks: in dogs, vagal stimulation strong enough to cause cardiac arrest produced no change in His-Purkinje conduction at all.)
  • Why atropine can make it worse: atropine has exactly one move — it raises the rate — and infranodal block is rate-dependent. Speed the sinus node and improve AV nodal conduction, and you deliver more impulses per minute into tissue whose only hope was having time to recover between them. The guideline says it plainly: the block "will likely worsen as the sinus rate increases." Faster atria, slower ventricles, sicker patient.
This is not theoretical. A 77-year-old with symptomatic 2:1 block received 600 mcg of IV atropine and deteriorated into ventricular standstill with loss of consciousness — rescued only with an adrenaline infusion and pacing (Armour, Br Paramedic J 2022). The guideline's own safety statement: atropine "should be used judiciously in patients with atrioventricular block and wide QRS complexes that suggest the presence of significant His-Purkinje disease."
The mechanism behind "atropine may worsen infranodal block" — and the mirror-image reason carotid sinus massage can transiently improve it.
The mirror image is a genuinely useful bedside test: vagal maneuvers worsen nodal block but transiently improve infranodal block, because slowing the sinus rate gives the sick His-Purkinje time to recover between beats. Exercise and atropine do the reverse. If a maneuver that should make things worse makes them better, you have localized the lesion.

And that converse is the proof that the mechanism is rate, not receptors. If atropine failed because the His-Purkinje had no muscarinic supply, then adding vagal tone with carotid massage should do precisely nothing to an infranodal block. It doesn't do nothing — it makes it better. Only a rate mechanism explains both directions. (Rate alone is sufficient, too: infra-His block can be produced in a normal His-Purkinje system just by pacing fast enough.)

5 · The blood supply — and the inferior-vs-anterior MI contrast

Two coronary facts do most of the clinical work here, and both are more nuanced than the usual teaching:

StructureSupply (verified)What it means at the bedside
SA nodeSA nodal artery from the RCA in ~68%, LCx in ~22% (pooled meta-analysis of 61 studies, n≈20,700 — Vikse, PLOS ONE 2016)Sinus bradycardia/arrest complicating a proximal RCA lesion. Note the SA nodal artery does not reliably track dominance.
AV nodeAV nodal artery arises from the dominant artery — essentially always. In right-dominant hearts it is right-origin in ~88%; population-wide, right-origin is only ~72% because not everyone is right-dominant (angiographic series, n=276)This is why inferior MI → AV block. The durable rule is "the AV nodal artery comes off the dominant vessel," which is more useful than any percentage.
His bundleDual supply — AV nodal artery and the first septal perforator of the LAD — in 9 of 10 hearts (Frink & James, Circulation 1973)Dual supply makes the His relatively protected — so infranodal block from ischemia implies a big anterior infarct.
Honesty about the numbersThe famous fascicular blood-supply percentages ("90% of cases… dual supply in 40–50%") trace back to a 10-heart necropsy series (Frink & James 1973). Every "10%" is literally one heart. The qualitative pattern is sound; the implied precision is not. Similarly, the commonly-taught "SA node: RCA 60% / LCx 40%" appears to be a conflation — the 40% is the entire left coronary contribution, of which the circumflex is only ~30%.
Inferior MI (RCA)Anterior MI (LAD)
LesionAV nodal artery ischemia + a big vagal (Bezold-Jarisch) surgeSeptal perforators → necrosis of the His-Purkinje system itself
LevelNodal (suprahisian)Infranodal
Pattern1° / Wenckebach, gradual onset, narrow escapeMobitz II → sudden complete block, wide escape
AtropineUsually worksUsually doesn't
CourseUsually transient — typically resolves within days; often no PPM neededOminous — marks a large infarct; frequently needs pacing
PrognosisBlock itself is rarely the problemBlock is a marker of infarct size; mortality is driven by the muscle lost
Reperfuse the artery, not the rhythm. In inferior MI, AV block that looks alarming on the monitor very often melts away once the RCA is open — and the single most important treatment for MI-associated AV block is revascularization, not a pacing wire.
The through-line for the rest of this guide. Every therapy below interrupts one specific step above. Atropine → blocks M₂, releasing the vagal brake on the SA and AV nodes (useless below the node). Dopamine / epinephrine / isoproterenol → β₁ → ↑cAMP → steepen phase 4 and speed AV nodal conduction. Glucagon → raises cAMP through a non-β receptor, which is why it works when the β receptor is occupied by a blocker. Calcium → floods the ICaL step that verapamil is blocking. DigiFab → removes digoxin from the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, cutting the vagotonic drive. Pacing → bypasses the entire broken cascade and imposes a rate from outside. That last one is the only therapy that always works — which is why the definitive treatment for bradycardia is a device, not a drug.

Presentation & findings — and why

🩺

Symptoms — frequency and the mechanism behind each

Every symptom here comes from one equation: cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume. Drop the rate and the ventricle compensates by filling longer and ejecting a bigger stroke volume — which is why a fit 40-year-old at 45 bpm feels nothing. Symptoms begin when that compensation runs out, and where the shortfall shows up decides what the patient complains about: brain → syncope, muscle → fatigue, lungs → dyspnea.

Read the percentages honestlyUnlike heart failure or pneumonia, bradycardia has no well-denominated symptom-frequency literature. Sources list the symptom set without denominators. Below, every number in the frequency column is a real, published figure with its source named; where no defensible number exists, the cell says so rather than inventing one. That gap is itself the teaching point — which is exactly why the guideline anchors everything to symptom–rhythm correlation instead of to a rate or a frequency table.

Sinus node dysfunction

Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Syncope~50%
of SND patients who received a PPM (2018 guideline §5.2, citing 1 trial)
An abrupt pause or sinus arrest drops cerebral perfusion below the autoregulatory floor. In tachy-brady it is classically the offset pause: the atrial tachycardia has been overdrive-suppressing an already-sick sinus node, so when it terminates the node is stunned and silent for seconds.
Tachy-brady syndrome≥50%
of SND patients (StatPearls)
The same diseased, fibrotic atrium that fails to pace also supports re-entry → AF/flutter alternating with bradycardia. This is the therapeutic trap: the drug you need for the tachycardia makes the bradycardia worse.
Chronotropic incompetence20–60%
of SND patients (StatPearls); 9–89% across all populations, ~⅓ of CHF (2018 guideline §4.2.2)
The node holds a resting rate but cannot accelerate — reduced If reserve and blunted β-responsiveness. Presents as exertional dyspnea and exercise intolerance, not as a low number on a resting ECG. The 9–89% spread is real and reflects the absence of a consensus definition.
Exertional dyspnea / exercise intoleranceListed as a manifestation; no published denominatorFixed cardiac output against rising metabolic demand → the patient hits an output ceiling. Usually the first symptom of chronotropic incompetence and the one most often dismissed as deconditioning or age.
Fatigue, lightheadedness, presyncopeListed as manifestations; no published denominatorChronic low-normal output → skeletal muscle and cerebral hypoperfusion. Notoriously nonspecific — the guideline explicitly warns "nonspecific symptoms such as fatigue can be multifactorial."
Asymptomatic / incidentalCommon but not quantifiedStroke-volume compensation is intact. Matters enormously: asymptomatic SND is a Class III: Harm indication for pacing — finding it is not a reason to treat it.

AV block — the ESC's qualitative distribution (§5.2.1)

FindingWhere it clustersWhy it happens
AsymptomaticFirst-degree AV block is "usually asymptomatic"Nothing is actually blocked — every P still conducts. It is an AV delay, not a block, which is why the guideline notes the name is a misnomer.
Syncope & dizziness"mainly observed in high-degree and complete AVB, especially the paroxysmal forms"Paroxysmal block is the dangerous phenotype: conduction is normal until it abruptly isn't, and the escape pacemaker takes seconds to wake up (Stokes-Adams attack). No prodrome, no warning, full-force fall.
Heart failure symptoms"more common in chronic AVB with permanent bradycardia"Sustained low output + loss of AV synchrony. Also seen in first-degree block if the PR is very long: the atrium contracts against a closed mitral valve → effective "pacemaker syndrome" without a pacemaker.
Fatigue, exertional intoleranceCommon — and the guideline warns they are "sometimes underestimated" given the advanced age at onsetAttributed to aging rather than to the rhythm. This is the single most common reason a pacemakeable patient goes unrecognized in clinic.
Cognitive decline"often only speculative"; improvement after PPM "unpredictable and unlikely"Chronic cerebral hypoperfusion is plausible but unproven. The ESC is unusually blunt here — do not promise a family that a pacemaker will restore cognition.
Death in untreated AV block is not only pump failure. Per the ESC: it is "due not only to HF secondary to low cardiac output, but also to SCD caused by prolonged asystole or bradycardia-triggered ventricular tachyarrhythmia." A long QT from a slow rate invites torsades — bradycardia kills through tachycardia. That is why you pace an asymptomatic Mobitz II.

Physical findings in complete heart block — the mechanism behind each

SignWhy it happens
Cannon A waves (irregular, intermittent)In AV dissociation the atrium contracts whenever it likes — sometimes against a closed tricuspid valve. The blood has nowhere to go but backwards up the jugular → a giant intermittent venous pulsation. Intermittent = dissociation. (Regular cannon A waves every beat = a junctional rhythm with retrograde conduction, a different animal.)
Variable S₁ intensityS₁ loudness depends on how far apart the mitral leaflets are when the ventricle contracts — which depends on the PR interval. In dissociation the PR is different every beat, so the leaflets start from a different position each time.
Wide pulse pressure / systolic hypertensionA long diastole = a huge filling volume = a big stroke volume (Frank-Starling) ejected into an aorta that has had ages to empty. Systolic BP climbs, diastolic falls. Do not "treat" this hypertension — it is a consequence of the rate, and it resolves when you fix the rhythm.
Intermittent systolic murmur variationBeat-to-beat stroke volume varies with the preceding filling time, so flow murmurs wax and wane.
Fixed, slow, regular pulse unresponsive to exertionThe ventricle is being driven by an escape focus with no autonomic responsiveness. The classic bedside tell: ask the patient to cough or lift their legs — the rate does not move.
📈

The ECG atlas — read these six and you can read bradycardia

The whole diagnosis lives on a rhythm strip. Work it in this fixed order and you will not get lost: (1) Is there a P for every QRS? (2) Is there a QRS for every P? (3) Is the PR constant, marching, or random? (4) Is the QRS narrow or wide?

The spectrum. Everything left of "Third degree" still has some conduction — that is what "incomplete" means, and it is why high-grade block (≥2 consecutive blocked P waves with evidence of some conduction) is not the same as complete block.
Image: CardioNetworks/Drj, CC BY-SA 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons
Sinus bradycardia, 45 bpm. Note the machine's own read: "Marked sinus bradycardia," PR 146 ms. Every P is followed by a QRS — the wiring is fine. The generator is just slow. This is SND territory, not AV block.
Image: Glenlarson, public domain — Wikimedia Commons
First-degree AV block (PR >200 ms). The guideline is pointed about this: it is "more accurately defined as atrioventricular delay because no P waves are blocked." Every impulse gets through — it just dawdles in the node.
Image: Andrewmeyerson, CC BY-SA 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons
Mobitz I (Wenckebach), 5:4. Look at the printed numbers: P-R marches 25 → 31 → 35 → 40 and then a P drops. The increment shrinks (6, 4, 5) even as the absolute PR grows — which is why the R-R intervals actually shorten before the pause. The laddergram underneath shows exactly where each impulse dies.
Image: Jason E. Roediger (Jer5150), CC BY-SA 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons
Mobitz II. Constant PR, then a P simply fails — no warning, no march. Definitionally this excludes 2:1. It "most often has a wide QRS," it is infranodal, and it is the one that gets a pacemaker regardless of symptoms.
Image: James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons
2:1 AV block — arrows mark every P. This is neither Mobitz I nor II and saying either is wrong: with only one conducted PR before each blocked P, you cannot show whether the PR was lengthening. It is a descriptive category that demands more information.
Image: James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons
Complete heart block with a junctional escape. The laddergram tells the story: every atrial impulse (top tier) dies in the AV tier, and the ventricle beats on its own schedule. P waves march through the QRS complexes, utterly indifferent to them. PR intervals are random, not long — that is the difference from first-degree block.
Image: Jason E. Roediger (Jer5150), CC BY-SA 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons
Complete heart block, 12-lead. Two independent rhythms: an atrial rate and a slower, regular ventricular rate with no relationship between them. Measure the P-P and the R-R separately — each is regular, and they ignore each other.
Image: James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons
AV dissociation ≠ complete heart block. Every complete block produces AV dissociation, but not every dissociation is block. If the ventricular rate is faster than the atrial rate, the AV node is not blocked — it is simply being beaten to the punch by a faster junctional or ventricular focus (isorhythmic dissociation, accelerated junctional rhythm). The test: in complete block the atria are faster than the ventricles and still fail to conduct. Pacing a dissociation that isn't block fixes nothing.
ECG clueSuggestsThe honest error rate (2018 guideline §6.4.3)
Narrow QRSNodal"there are instances where it has been determined to be infranodal during an EPS"
Mobitz I + narrow QRSNodal"in some cases Mobitz type I… and an associated narrow QRS can be attributable to infranodal block" — and when it is, "a pacemaker may be considered even in the absence of symptoms"
2nd-degree AVB + bundle branch blockInfranodal"likely but not necessarily (70% likelihood)"
2:1 AVB + bundle branch blockInfranodal"however, 15% to 20% of these patients can have block in the AV node" — so ~80–85% infranodal, not 100%
Severe 1° AVB (PR >300 ms) + narrow QRSNodal"usually indicates atrioventricular node delay"
Blocked P with simultaneous P-P slowingVagal / functionalVagally mediated block "can be recognized by the presence of concomitant sinus node slowing (P-P prolongation)." A dropped P on a rock-steady P-P argues against a vagal mechanism.
Block appears when the rate slowsInfranodal (brady-dependent)ESC 2021: supports "a diagnosis of intrinsic infranodal AVB"
Mobitz II is "a commonly overdiagnosed and misinterpreted arrhythmia" — the usual error is calling 2:1 block "Mobitz II" and committing the patient to a device. Before you page EP, find a stretch of the strip with two consecutive conducted beats. If you cannot, you cannot call it Mobitz II.
🔬

The reversible causes — and why each lab moves

The guideline makes hunting reversible causes a Class I (C-EO) step before anything else. Nearly all of them are found with a 12-lead, a chemistry panel, a TSH, and a medication list.

TestWhat moves, and the mechanismWhat raises / lowers it falsely
Potassium↑K⁺ depolarizes the resting membrane → fewer available Na⁺ channels → ↓Vmax → slowed infranodal conduction, widening QRS, then sine wave. Peaked T waves are a separate mechanism (accelerated repolarization via ↑IKr) — do not merge the two.Pseudohyperkalemia from hemolysis, fist-clenching during draw, prolonged tourniquet, marked leukocytosis/thrombocytosis. Redraw before you treat a number that doesn't fit the patient.
TSH↑TSH / hypothyroidism → reduced β-receptor density and blunted catecholamine responsiveness + directly reduced sinus node automaticity → sinus bradycardia, low voltage, prolonged QT.Non-thyroidal illness ("sick euthyroid") distorts TSH in acute illness; amiodarone can drive thyroid dysfunction both ways — and cause bradycardia directly.
Digoxin levelDigoxin inhibits Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and is powerfully vagotonic → slows SA and AV nodal conduction. Classic toxicity rhythm: atrial tachycardia with block, or regularized AF (= junctional rhythm).Draw ≥6–8 h post-dose or the level is falsely high (distribution phase). Toxicity occurs at "normal" levels when K⁺ is low, Mg²⁺ is low, or Ca²⁺ is high. After DigiFab, total levels are uninterpretable — the assay measures bound drug.
TroponinRises with the ischemia that caused the block (and it is a +2 variable on the Canadian Syncope Risk Score).Bradycardia and demand ischemia alone can bump troponin without epicardial occlusion. Also elevated in CKD, myocarditis, PE. A trivial bump in a bradycardic patient is not automatically an MI.
Magnesium / calciumHypomagnesemia potentiates digoxin toxicity and refractory arrhythmia; severe hypercalcemia shortens the QT and can cause bradyarrhythmia and AV block.Serum Mg²⁺ correlates poorly with total body stores — a "normal" Mg can coexist with real depletion. Correct calcium for albumin.
Lyme serologyTwo-tier testing (EIA → immunoblot). Borrelia-driven inflammation of the conduction system → AV block, characteristically fluctuating over minutes to hours and typically reversible.Serology is often negative early in disseminated disease; in an endemic area with a compatible story, do not let a negative EIA stop you. Conversely IgG stays positive for years after treated disease.
Sleep studyApnea → hypoxemia + a massive vagal surge → profound nocturnal bradycardia and AV block. The signature: progressive bradycardia during the apnea, then tachycardia and hypertension at arousal.Nocturnal bradycardia is physiologic in the young and in athletes — the guideline says pauses >5 s are "common" in rest/sleep. Don't call a normal athlete's night an apnea.
Severe hyperkalemia. Broad, bizarre, blurred complexes losing their distinction between QRS and T — the pre-terminal sine-wave morphology. This is a sodium-channel problem produced by a potassium number.
Image: Michael Rosengarten BEng, MD, McGill (CardioNetworks ECGpedia), CC BY-SA 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons
Hypothermia with Osborn (J) waves — the notch at the J point. Hypothermia slows the sinus node directly and is atropine-resistant: the fix is rewarming, not drugs. Handle the patient gently; a cold myocardium fibrillates easily.
Image: WikiSysop, CC BY 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons
The ECG is a poor test for hyperkalemia — reported sensitivity is roughly 34–43%, rising only to ~55–62% when K⁺ >6.5 mmol/L. A near-normal ECG does not exclude a lethal potassium, and patients have arrested with unremarkable tracings. The published K⁺-vs-finding thresholds vary by a full 1–1.5 mmol/L between reputable sources; they are traditional, not evidentiary. Treat the number and the patient — never the tracing alone.

When to suspect

🔍

Who walks in with this

Bradycardia in clinic arrives three ways: an incidental slow rate on a routine ECG, a fall or blackout, or "I'm just tired" in someone over 70 whose fatigue everyone has been attributing to age.

EpidemiologyNumberSource
Incidence of sick sinus syndrome, general population0.8 per 1,000 person-years (95% CI 0.7–0.9)ARIC + CHS pooled, n=20,572, ~17 y follow-up (Jensen, JACC 2014)
Effect of ageHR 1.73 per 5-year increment (1.47–2.05)Same. SND is fundamentally a disease of aging — most common in the 70s–80s.
Mean age at SND diagnosis68 years; men = womenStatPearls
Annual incidence of complete AV block within SND0–4.5%, median 0.6%StatPearls — low, which is why SND alone doesn't earn a prophylactic pacer
Syncope attributable to bradycardia/conduction disease at first presentation~10% (+ ~18% neurally mediated)2018 guideline §4.2.1
Diagnostic yield of the initial ECG in syncope~5%2018 guideline §4.2.1 — which is exactly why monitoring exists
The only question that matters in clinic: is the bradycardia causing the symptom? The guideline's definition of symptomatic bradycardia is "a documented bradyarrhythmia that is directly responsible for… syncope or presyncope, transient dizziness or lightheadedness, heart failure symptoms, or confusional states." It then concedes: "Direct attribution of bradycardia as the sole source of symptoms is challenging." Your whole outpatient job is establishing that link — because "there is no established minimum heart rate below which treatment is indicated."
The athlete trap. Sinus bradycardia to ≥30 bpm, PR 200–400 ms, Mobitz I, and junctional escape are all normal, training-related findings in an asymptomatic athlete and need no workup (International Criteria, JACC 2017). First-degree block appears on 24-h Holter in 27.5–40% of athletes and Wenckebach in 15–22%. The discriminator is one sentence: "Sinus rhythm should resume and bradycardia should resolve with the onset of physical activity." Walk them down the hall. What is abnormal: HR <30, pause ≥3 s on a resting ECG, PR ≥400 ms, Mobitz II, or complete block.
A correction worth carrying"Athlete's bradycardia is high vagal tone" is incomplete. Four independent human autonomic-blockade studies show the intrinsic heart rate is lower in athletes even after full atropine + β-blockade — i.e., the sinus node itself is remodeled (If/HCN4 downregulation), not merely braked. The 2018 guideline still files athletic conditioning under "vagotonic"; the mechanism is now understood to be both. Animal data conflict on direction (rodents: HCN4 down; dogs: HCN4 up), so state it as vagal tone plus intrinsic remodeling.
Workup

What to order & when

🧪

Labs & imaging

12-lead ECGEvery patient, always. Establishes rate, level of block, QRS width, and conduction disease (BBB/fascicular). Class I in the syncope guideline. But remember it is diagnostic in only ~5% of syncope — a normal ECG proves nothing.Always
BMP (K⁺, Ca²⁺) + Mg²⁺Every patient. Hyperkalemia is the reversible cause you cannot afford to miss — and it is cheap.Always
TSHEvery patient with unexplained bradycardia. Hypothyroidism is common, reversible, and slows the node directly.Always
Medication reviewNot a lab, but the highest-yield "test" you will run. See the drugs-to-avoid table below. Include eye drops (timolol), OTC agents, and anything started in the last 3 months.Always
Digoxin levelIf they take it. Draw ≥6–8 h post-dose. Remember toxicity at "therapeutic" levels when K⁺ is low.If on digoxin
EchocardiogramIf structural disease is suspected, if there is conduction disease with syncope, or before device implant. AV block as a cause of syncope is far likelier with structural heart disease (34% vs 13% — 2018 guideline §6.4.3).Most patients
Lyme serologyEndemic area + compatible exposure/story, especially a young patient with new AV block. Fluctuating block is the tell.If suggestive
Sleep studyNocturnal bradyarrhythmia. Treating the apnea "eliminates the need for pacemaker implantation in most patients" — CPAP cuts profound bradycardia/pauses/AV block by 72–89%, and 86% stayed symptom-free without a pacer over 22 months. Class I (B-NR) for CPAP if OSA + bradycardia.If nocturnal
Cardiac MRI / FDG-PETUnexplained high-grade AV block in a younger patient → hunt for cardiac sarcoidosis or giant-cell myocarditis before you just implant a box. Finding sarcoid changes the device (ICD, not PPM) and adds immunosuppression. The specific age cut-off — "all patients <60 years of age who present with high-degree AV block should be screened for cardiac sarcoidosis" — is from the 2014 HRS expert consensus on arrhythmias in sarcoidosis (Birnie), not from the bradycardia guideline, which contains no such cutoff.If young / unexplained
Genetic testingConduction disease in a young patient with a family history: SCN5A (progressive cardiac conduction disease), LMNA (conduction disease that precedes cardiomyopathy), DMPK (myotonic dystrophy), HCN4. Changes the device decision toward an ICD.Selected

Choosing the monitor — match the device to the symptom frequency

This is the single most-botched outpatient decision in bradycardia. A 48-hour Holter for once-a-month syncope is a guaranteed non-diagnostic test. Match the recording window to how often the symptom actually happens:

Symptom frequencyRight toolWhy
Daily24–48 h HolterContinuous, cheap, captures a daily event with near-certainty. Also the tool for quantifying burden (pause count, AF burden).
Every few days → weeklyPatch / event monitor, 14–30 daysLong enough to catch a weekly event; patch adherence is far better than a Holter's wires.
Monthly or less, or unexplained syncopeImplantable loop recorder (ILR)Up to ~3 years of monitoring. This is the answer for infrequent, high-stakes events. In syncope with a normal ECG and echo, 8% were found to have paroxysmal idiopathic AV block (2018 guideline §6.2) — you will never catch that on a Holter.
Exertional symptomsExercise treadmill testThe only way to diagnose chronotropic incompetence — and it doubles as the nodal-vs-infranodal test: exercise improves nodal block and worsens infranodal block.
Suspected reflex/vasovagalTilt table (ESC Class IIa B)"Tilt testing should be considered in patients with suspected recurrent reflex syncope."

Chronotropic incompetence — the arithmetic

The literature's most common definition: failure to reach 80% of expected heart rate reserve on exercise (2018 guideline §2.2, Table 3).




—
Enter age, resting HR and peak HR.
The guideline's own caveats — include them"Although this definition has been used in literature, in practice, specifically defining chronotropic incompetence is difficult." Others favour 220 − 0.7 × age as a better predictor, and sex and comorbidity matter. The guideline's conclusion: the diagnosis "requires careful individualized clinical assessment and probably cannot be determined by age alone." Use this number as a prompt to think, not as a verdict.

When to send for an EP study

Reserve it for the case where the symptom and the rhythm won't line up non-invasively — typically syncope with bifascicular block or a suspected paroxysmal infranodal block. The number to know is the HV interval:

HV intervalMeaning4-year progression to AV block
<70 msNormal4%
70–100 msAbnormal — the pacing threshold12%
>100 msMarkedly abnormal24%

Progression gradient per Scheinman, cited in the 2021 ESC pacing guideline.

Get the two HV numbers straight — they are constantly conflated. ≥70 ms is the baseline threshold that carries a pacing recommendation (ACC/AHA COR I, C-LD with syncope; ESC Class I, B). ≥100 ms is the post-provocation threshold — ESC: "HV ≥70 ms, or HV ≥100 ms after pharmacological stress (ajmaline, procainamide, flecainide, or disopyramide)." The 2018 ACC/AHA guideline never mentions 100 ms at all. Writing "HV ≥100 ms is the pacing indication" is a checkable error.
  • In myotonic dystrophy, 46.7% of patients with an HV ≥70 ms went on to develop high-grade AV block (2018 guideline §6.4.4) — and in that population, HV ≥70 ms alone earns a Class I pacemaker regardless of symptoms, versus the general population where the same number requires syncope. Same threshold, symptom requirement dropped.
  • In syncope + BBB/bifascicular block, 61% had a significant His-Purkinje abnormality at EPS (§6.2).
  • EPS diagnostic yield overall: 12–80%, "depending on the patient population studied" — a range that tells you patient selection is everything.
  • EPS also unmasks His bundle extrasystoles, a classic mimic that looks exactly like AV block on the surface ECG.
  • Procainamide challenge: a 15-ms increase in HV or induced infranodal block is abnormal — but the guideline warns "the sensitivity of a procainamide challenge for distal conduction disease is low." A negative test does not clear them.
Treat

Chronic management

💊

Stepwise therapy — first-line → escalation

There is no chronic oral drug that treats bradycardia. This is the defining fact of the topic and it makes the ladder look unlike every other guide in this library. Rung 1 is subtraction (stop the culprit), rung 2 is fixing the cause, and rung 3 is a device. The only oral agent with any guideline standing is theophylline, and it is Class IIb — used as a diagnostic trial to see whether raising the rate helps, not as destination therapy.
1
Remove the culprit drug & correct reversible causes
Class I (C-EO) — and it fixes a large share of cases outright.
▾
Every one of these drugs works by interrupting a step in the cascade you read above. Stopping it restores the step. The guideline: "Negative chronotropic drugs exacerbate SND symptoms by diminishing the slope of phase 4 diastolic depolarization."
CulpritMechanism it blocksLevel hitWhat to do
β-blockers
metoprolol, atenolol, carvedilol, bisoprolol, timolol eye drops, sotalol		Removes cAMP-driven augmentation of If + ICaL (does not block Ca channels directly)SA + AV nodeHalve the dose or hold. Check the eye drops — timolol is systemically absorbed and is a classic missed cause. If HFrEF needs the β-blocker, that is a pacing indication (Class I, C-LD), not a reason to stop it.
Non-DHP CCBs
diltiazem, verapamil		Blocks ICaL — the AV node's actual upstroke currentSA + AV nodeStop. Switch to a dihydropyridine (amlodipine) if you needed the BP control — DHPs have no meaningful nodal effect.
DigoxinNa⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition → strongly vagotonicSA + AV nodeStop; check a level and the K⁺. Toxicity happens at "normal" levels if K⁺ low / Mg²⁺ low / Ca²⁺ high.
Amiodarone, sotalol, dronedaroneClass III + intrinsic β-blocking (amiodarone) propertiesSA + AV nodeAmiodarone's half-life is weeks to months — stopping it today does not fix the rate this week. Plan accordingly.
Class Ic
flecainide, propafenone		Fast Na⁺ channel block → slows His-Purkinje conduction, widens QRSInfranodal (and some nodal)Contraindicated with pre-existing 2°/3° block, SND, or BBB. Caution if baseline QRS >130 ms.
IvabradineBlocks If directly — bradycardia is the on-target effect, not a side effectSA nodeBradycardia 6.0% per patient-year vs 1.3% on placebo (FDA label). Contraindicated in SND and existing conduction disease.
Cholinesterase inhibitors
donepezil, rivastigmine, pyridostigmine		↑synaptic ACh → more M₂ drive → the vagal brake, harderSA + AV nodeGenuinely under-recognized: the dementia patient with syncope on donepezil. Stop it and watch.
Clonidine, dexmedetomidineCentral α₂ agonism → ↓sympathetic outflowSA nodeTaper clonidine — abrupt stop causes rebound hypertension.
S1P modulators
fingolimod, siponimod, ozanimod		S1P₁ receptor engagement on atrial myocytes activates GIRK/IKACh — the same channel the vagus opensSA + AV nodeFirst-dose observation is a labeled requirement. The effect is largest with the first dose and attenuates.
Lithium, opioids, propofol, lacosamideVarious — lithium is directly SA-node toxic; lacosamide prolongs PRSA / AV nodeCheck a lithium level. Review the whole anesthetic record if this started peri-op.
The "necessary drug" clause — know this one cold. Removing the culprit does not automatically remove the pacing indication. The guideline is explicit (Class I, C-LD): "In patients who develop symptomatic AV block as a consequence of guideline-directed management and therapy for which there is no alternative treatment and continued treatment is clinically necessary, permanent pacing is recommended." Translation: if your HFrEF patient needs their β-blocker and it makes them block, you pace them so they can keep the β-blocker. You do not sacrifice mortality-reducing therapy to protect a heart rate.
And the converse: finding a reversible cause doesn't always mean treating it. The guideline's own example — stopping a β-blocker in an asymptomatic patient with sinus bradycardia after STEMI "may not be necessary."
You don't always have to wait out the washout. A separate recommendation (IIa, B-NR) closes the loop: in patients "on chronic stable doses of medically necessary antiarrhythmic or beta-blocker therapy, it is reasonable to proceed to permanent pacing without further observation for drug washout or reversibility." The logic: if they've been on a stable dose for years and only now block, the drug didn't suddenly change — they did. The conduction disease is structural and the drug merely unmasked it. This spares the patient a pointless week of telemetry waiting for a washout that will not change the answer.
2
Treat the underlying disease
Sleep apnea, thyroid, Lyme, ischemia, sarcoid.
▾
  • Sleep apnea → CPAP. The highest-yield "cure" in this whole section. CPAP reduces profound sinus bradycardia, pauses and AV block by 72–89%; 86% stayed free of bradyarrhythmia symptoms without a pacemaker over 22 months. The guideline: "Treating the underlying sleep apnea… eliminates the need for pacemaker implantation in most patients." Class I (B-NR) for CPAP in OSA + bradycardia; Class IIa (B-NR) to screen for apnea if you are considering a pacer.
  • Hypothyroidism → levothyroxine. Reverses over weeks. Start low in the elderly/CAD.
  • Lyme carditis → antibiotics. AV block is usually at the nodal level, fluctuates by the hour, and is typically fully reversible — most patients recover conduction and do not need a permanent device. A temporary wire may be needed as a bridge; a PPM implanted in the first days is often a device the patient never needed.
  • Ischemia → revascularize. In inferior MI the block usually follows the artery: open the RCA and the rhythm frequently follows.
  • Cardiac sarcoid → immunosuppression + a device — and note the device is usually an ICD, not a plain pacemaker, because the arrhythmic death is ventricular.
3
Permanent pacemaker — the definitive therapy
Verbatim indications with COR/LOE.
▾
Pacing doesn't repair the cascade — it bypasses it, delivering a depolarization from outside the diseased tissue. That is why it is the one therapy that always works, and why it is the answer for structural conduction disease.

Sinus node dysfunction (2018 guideline §5.4.4)

CORLOERecommendation (verbatim / condensed)
IC-LD"In patients with symptoms that are directly attributable to SND, permanent pacing is indicated to increase heart rate and improve symptoms."
IC-EOSymptomatic sinus bradycardia as a consequence of guideline-directed therapy with no alternative and continued treatment clinically necessary → pacing recommended.
IIaC-EOTachy-brady syndrome with symptoms attributable to the bradycardia → pacing reasonable.
IIaC-EOSymptomatic chronotropic incompetence → pacing with rate-responsive programming is reasonable.
IIbC-LDSymptoms likely attributable to SND → a trial of oral theophylline may be considered, to improve symptoms and to help determine the potential effects of permanent pacing.
Class III: Harm (C-LD) — do NOT pace: asymptomatic sinus bradycardia or pauses secondary to physiologically elevated vagal tone; sleep-related sinus bradycardia or transient pauses during sleep (unless another indication exists); asymptomatic SND. The benefit of pacing in SND is quality of life, not survival — an asymptomatic patient has no quality of life to gain and inherits every device complication.

AV block (2018 guideline §6.4.4)

CORLOERecommendation (verbatim / condensed)
IB-NR"In patients with acquired second-degree Mobitz type II atrioventricular block, high-grade atrioventricular block, or third-degree atrioventricular block not attributable to reversible or physiologic causes, permanent pacing is recommended regardless of symptoms."
IB-NRNeuromuscular disease (myotonic dystrophy type 1, Kearns-Sayre) with 2°, 3° block, or HV ≥70 ms, regardless of symptoms → pacing (± defibrillator if needed), if meaningful survival >1 y expected.
IC-LDPermanent AF with symptomatic bradycardia → pacing recommended.
IC-LDSymptomatic AV block from necessary guideline-directed therapy with no alternative → pacing recommended.
IIaB-NRInfiltrative cardiomyopathy (cardiac sarcoidosis, amyloidosis) + Mobitz II / high-grade / third-degree block → pacing with defibrillator capability if needed is reasonable.
IIaB-NRLamin A/C mutations (incl. limb-girdle, Emery-Dreifuss) with PR >240 ms AND LBBB → pacing ± ICD is reasonable.
IIaC-LDMarked first-degree or Mobitz I block with symptoms clearly attributable to the block → pacing reasonable.
IIbC-LDNeuromuscular disease (e.g. DM1) with PR >240 ms, QRS >120 ms, or fascicular block → pacing ± ICD may be considered.
The asymmetry that defines this topic. In SND, symptoms are everything — no symptoms, no pacer. In AV block, the guideline breaks that rule: "unlike SND, infranodal atrioventricular block regardless of the presence or absence of symptoms warrants a pacemaker because the patient could suffer from sudden" collapse. The justification is one sentence from §6.4.1: patients with infranodal disease who progress to complete block "will be dependent on unreliable ventricular escape rhythms." You are not pacing the rate. You are insuring against the escape failing.
Neuromuscular disease gets its own rules — and they are aggressive. Myotonic dystrophy type 1 earns a Class I pacemaker at 2°/3° block or an HV ≥70 ms alone, regardless of symptoms. Why: conduction disease occurs in ~90%, "fatal arrhythmias can occur prior to other symptoms," and >50% of DM1 patients with a normal ECG have infra-Hisian block at EPS. In DM1 a severe ECG abnormality carried a relative risk of 3.30 for sudden death (Groh, NEJM 2008). Elegant mechanism: DM1 mis-splices SCN5A back to a fetal Nav1.5 isoform — converging on the same sodium-channel loss-of-function as hereditary Lenègre disease.
⚙️

Which pacemaker — mode selection & the RV pacing problem

Choosing the device is a second decision, and getting it wrong causes iatrogenic heart failure.

ModeMeansUse whenWatch out
DDD(R)Sense + pace both chambersDefault for AV block, and for SND with any conduction diseaseProgram a long AV delay / AV-search hysteresis to avoid needless RV pacing
AAI(R)Atrium onlyPure SND with intact AV conductionRarely used alone in the US — risk of later AV block leaves the ventricle unprotected. DANPACE found AAIR had more AF and more reoperations than DDDR with no survival difference, which killed the single-lead strategy.
VVI(R)Ventricle onlyPermanent AF with symptomatic bradycardia; or a frail patient where a single lead is the goalIn sinus rhythm it causes pacemaker syndrome — the atrium contracts against closed AV valves → cannon A waves, fatigue, hypotension. That is the same mechanism as complete heart block, now iatrogenic.
Rate-responsive (R)Accelerometer/minute-ventilation sensor drives the rateChronotropic incompetence (IIa)Pointless if the patient's own rate response is intact
Why "less RV pacing" became a design goal. An RV apical lead depolarizes the ventricle from an abnormal site — functionally creating an LBBB. The septum contracts before the free wall, the ventricle wrings inefficiently, and over years that dyssynchrony remodels into a cardiomyopathy. DAVID made this unmissable: in ICD patients with LV dysfunction, dual-chamber pacing at DDDR-70 was worse than backup VVI-40 — more death and HF hospitalization from pacing they didn't need. The lesson: RV pacing is not benign, and pacing a ventricle that doesn't need it causes harm.
When RV pacing is the wrong answer — and the two societies use different numbers. Do not blend them:
SocietyThresholdRecommendationClass / Level
2018 ACC/AHA/HRSLVEF 36–50% and expected ventricular pacing >40%CRT or His-bundle pacing rather than an RV leadIIa, B-R
2018 ACC/AHA/HRSSame EF band but expected pacing <40%RV pacing is preferred over CRT/HBP — the mirror recommendation, and the one everyone forgetsIIa, B-R
2021 ESCLVEF <40% + high-degree AV blockCRT rather than RV pacingI, A (upgraded from IIa in 2013)
Where the numbers come from: the 40% pacing threshold is from MOST — per the ESC, "at least 40% RV pacing is associated with an increased risk of HF hospitalization or AF." The LVEF band is from BLOCK-HF (n=691, EF ≤50% by inclusion, mean 42.9%, 37 months), which showed biventricular pacing beat RV pacing on death / HF urgent care / LV remodeling. Two different trials, two different variables — that is why the recommendation has two conditions.
Currency flag — read this before quoting a class on His/left bundle pacingConduction system pacing (His-bundle and left bundle branch area pacing) captures the native His-Purkinje system and produces a narrow, physiologic QRS — mechanistically the most attractive way to pace someone who will be paced constantly. LBBAP is technically easier than His pacing with better, more stable thresholds. But the 2021 ESC pacing guideline gave LBBAP no formal recommendation, explicitly deferring pending randomized trials. Since then: the 2023 HRS/APHRS/LAHRS guideline on cardiac physiologic pacing for the avoidance and mitigation of heart failure (Heart Rhythm 2023;20(9):e17–e91) addresses it — note its scope is CPP for heart failure, not conduction system pacing generally. A 2025 ESC document on CSP exists but is a Clinical Consensus Statement, not a guideline — don't quote it with guideline-level COR/LOE. This guide is written in 2026: treat CSP as established and fast-moving, and verify the current class before you quote one.
Monitor

Follow-up cadence

📈

What to recheck, and when

SituationCadenceWhat you're looking for
After stopping/reducing a culprit drugRecheck ECG + symptoms in 2–4 weeks (longer for amiodarone — half-life is weeks to months)Did the rate recover? If yes, no device. If no, the conduction disease is structural.
Asymptomatic conduction disease (BBB, 1° block)Annual ECG + symptom reviewProgression to higher-grade block; new syncope
After starting levothyroxineTSH at 6 weeksRate response tracks thyroid normalization
After CPAP for OSA-related bradycardiaRepeat monitoring after adherent therapyResolution — this is what lets you avoid the pacemaker
Post-implant wound checkEarly, per your implanting service's protocolHematoma, infection, lead dislodgement, arm-restriction compliance. (Specific day-intervals vary by center — follow your device clinic's pathway rather than a number from a study guide.)
Ongoing device follow-upAnchor on remote monitoring — see the ESC recommendations belowThresholds, lead impedance, battery, ventricular pacing percentage, AF burden
ClassLevelESC 2021 device follow-up recommendation
IARemote device management is recommended to reduce the number of in-office follow-ups.
ICRemote monitoring is recommended for a device with a component under advisory/recall.
IIaA"In-office routine follow-up of single- and dual-chamber pacemakers may be spaced by up to 24 months in patients on remote device management."
IIaBRemote management should be considered for earlier detection of problems.

Follow-up recommendations from the 2021 ESC pacing guideline. The headline change is that remote monitoring, not the calendar, now drives the cadence — an in-office visit every 24 months is acceptable for a remotely-monitored single/dual-chamber pacemaker. Increase frequency near end of battery life.

Check the ventricular pacing percentage at every device visit. It is the single most actionable number on the interrogation. A patient paced 90% of the time who only needed backup pacing is being slowly given a cardiomyopathy — reprogram the AV delay.
Driving. Syncope of undetermined cause and unrepaired symptomatic bradycardia carry driving restrictions, and post-implant restrictions apply too. The specifics are state/jurisdiction-dependent and change — look up your own state's rule rather than quoting a number. Document the conversation.
Interactions

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

🔗

How each comorbidity changes the course AND the management

ComorbidityHow it changes the courseHow it changes management
HFrEFThe patient needs the exact drugs (β-blocker) that cause the bradycardia. Bradycardia also worsens output.Pace them so they can keep GDMT (Class I, C-LD). If EF ≤50% and pacing burden will be high → CRT/CSP, not RV pacing (BLOCK-HF). Never trade mortality-reducing therapy for a heart rate.
Atrial fibrillationTachy-brady: the same sick atrium fibrillates and fails to pace. Offset pauses cause the syncope.The trap: rate control worsens the bradycardia. Often the pacemaker enables the rate-control drug. Permanent AF + symptomatic bradycardia → pacing (Class I, C-LD), usually VVIR. Refractory: AV node ablation + pace — but this makes them pacemaker-dependent, permanently and irreversibly.
CKDHyperkalemia risk (a reversible cause that recurs); reduced digoxin clearance.Check K⁺ every time. Renally dose digoxin, sotalol, dofetilide. Contrast/venous access planning for implant; higher device infection risk.
OSAProfound nocturnal bradycardia and AV block — often entirely reversible.Treat the apnea first. This is the comorbidity most likely to let you avoid a device altogether.
HypothyroidismBlunts β-responsiveness and slows the node directly.Replace before committing to a device. Recheck TSH at 6 weeks.
Cardiac sarcoidosisGranulomas in the basal septum — where the conduction system lives. Young patient with unexplained high-grade block until proven otherwise.MRI/PET before implant. Immunosuppression. The device is usually an ICD (IIa, B-NR) — the mortality is ventricular arrhythmia, not the block.
Neuromuscular disease (DM1, Kearns-Sayre, Emery-Dreifuss)Aggressive, unpredictable, sudden progression. ~90% have conduction defects; fatal arrhythmias can precede other symptoms.Lowest pacing threshold in the guideline — Class I at 2°/3° block or HV ≥70 ms, regardless of symptoms. Consider ICD capability. Screen annually with ECG.
LMNA cardiomyopathyConduction disease comes first, cardiomyopathy later — sometimes by decades. Conduction disturbance in 81% of carriers; high malignant-arrhythmia rate.PR >240 ms + LBBB → pacing ± ICD (IIa, B-NR). A young patient with new conduction block and a family history of "heart failure" or sudden death deserves genetic testing before you implant a plain pacer.
Prior TAVR / valve surgeryMechanical injury to the adjacent His/left bundle. New LBBB and high-grade block are the classic complications.Post-procedure conduction monitoring; delayed block occurs. See the ICU panel.
Heart transplantDenervated → the resting rate runs high and there is no vagal brake to release.Atropine is Class III: Harm — it caused paradoxical heart block or sinus arrest in 20% of transplant patients in one 25-patient study. Use aminophylline or theophylline instead (guideline Table 8), or pace.
Dementia / frailty / limited prognosisSymptoms are hard to attribute; falls are multifactorial.Every device recommendation in the guideline is conditioned on "meaningful survival of greater than 1 year is expected." Pacing improves QOL in SND, not survival. Have the goals conversation before the referral.
Endurance athleteBradycardia, 1° block and Wenckebach are training adaptations, not disease.Resist the workup. Confirm the rate rises with activity. Class III: Harm to pace physiologic vagal bradycardia.
Drugs to avoid / use with real caution in known conduction disease: β-blockers (including timolol eye drops) · diltiazem, verapamil · digoxin · amiodarone, sotalol, dronedarone · class Ic (flecainide, propafenone) — contraindicated with 2°/3° block, SND or BBB · ivabradine — contraindicated in SND/conduction defects · adenosine — causes transient AV block/asystole by design; effect is markedly potentiated by dipyridamole and carbamazepine and exaggerated in the denervated (transplant) heart · clonidine, dexmedetomidine · donepezil, rivastigmine, pyridostigmine, neostigmine · fingolimod/siponimod/ozanimod (first-dose observation required) · lithium · opioids, propofol · lacosamide (PR prolongation).

The combination that catches people: a β-blocker plus diltiazem/verapamil. Each is tolerable alone; together they hit the same node from two directions and produce block far out of proportion to either dose. Also verapamil + digoxin — verapamil raises digoxin levels via P-glycoprotein inhibition, so a stable digoxin dose becomes toxic without anyone changing it.
Scores

Risk calculator

🧮

Canadian Syncope Risk Score — does this syncope need admission?

Bradycardia most often announces itself as syncope, and the hard question is disposition. The CSRS is the best-validated tool for it: derived in 4,030 patients (CMAJ 2016) and validated in 3,819 (JAMA Intern Med 2020) with an AUC of 0.91 and a calibration slope of 1.0.

Use it inPatients ≥16 years presenting within 24 hours of syncope. Do NOT use if: prolonged (>5 min) LOC, change in mental status from baseline, witnessed seizure, major trauma, intoxication, language barrier, or head trauma causing the LOC.
Clinical evaluation
Predisposition to vasovagal symptoms −1
History of heart disease +1
Any systolic BP <90 or >180 mm Hg +2
Investigations
Elevated troponin (>99th percentile) +2
Abnormal QRS axis (<−30° or >100°) +1
QRS duration >130 ms +1
QTc >480 ms +2
ED diagnosis (pick one)
Neither 0
Vasovagal syncope −2
Cardiac syncope +2
Range −3 to +11. The ED-diagnosis rows are mutually exclusive — the score requires the treating physician's diagnostic impression, which is the instrument's most-criticized feature. It is a decision aid, not an oracle.
0
RiskScore30-day serious outcomen
Very low−3 to −20.2%3 / 1,631
Low−1 to 00.7%9 / 1,254
Medium1 to 38.0%55 / 687
High4 to 519.2%32 / 167
Very high≥651.3%40 / 78

Risk percentages from the multicenter ED validation (n=3,819) — Thiruganasambandamoorthy, JAMA Intern Med 2020. Serious adverse event = death, arrhythmia, MI, serious structural heart disease, aortic dissection, PE, severe pulmonary hypertension, severe hemorrhage, SAH, or another serious condition causing the syncope / requiring intervention. Cross-check any individual patient at MDCalc.

Note what the score does not do: it predicts 30-day serious outcomes, not "is this bradycardia." Two of its seven variables (QRS duration, QRS axis) are conduction-disease markers — which is precisely why a syncope patient with a wide QRS scores badly. The score is quietly telling you to look at the conduction system.

Other scores you may see, and why they are not reimplemented here: the EGSYS score and the San Francisco Syncope Rule (CHESS) are both used for syncope, but their point values were not verified to a primary source during this build, so they are linked rather than guessed: EGSYS (MDCalc) · SFSR (MDCalc). Bradycardia itself has no validated severity score — there is no "CURB-65 for heart block." The guideline substitutes a question: are the symptoms attributable to the rhythm, and is the block infranodal?

Prevent

USPSTF A/B & prevention

🛡️

Grade A & B screening for this population

The bradycardia patient is typically an older adult with cardiovascular risk, and — importantly — at risk of falling. These are the recommendations that actually apply:

GradeRecommendationPopulation
AScreen for hypertension with office BP; confirm outside the clinic before starting treatmentAdults ≥18 y
AAsk all adults about tobacco use; advise cessation; offer behavioral + pharmacotherapyAll adults
BStatin for primary prevention of CVDAdults 40–75 y with ≥1 CVD risk factor and estimated 10-y risk ≥10%
BScreen for abdominal aortic aneurysm once by ultrasoundMen 65–75 y who have ever smoked
BExercise interventions to prevent fallsCommunity-dwelling adults ≥65 y at increased fall risk — directly relevant: bradycardia causes falls, and a "mechanical fall" in an older adult may be an unwitnessed syncope
BScreen for prediabetes and type 2 diabetesAdults 35–70 y with overweight/obesity
The two negative recommendations that matter most here — and they cut against instinct.
• Screening ECG in asymptomatic adults: Grade D for those at low risk of cardiovascular events (and Grade I — insufficient evidence — at intermediate/high risk). The USPSTF concluded the harms of screening ECG (false positives → downstream testing, invasive procedures) meet or exceed the benefit. This is exactly how an asymptomatic 40-bpm athlete ends up in an EP clinic.
• Screening for atrial fibrillation with ECG: Grade I — insufficient evidence (2022). Relevant because tachy-brady lives at the AF/SND intersection.
The unifying lesson: incidentally-detected asymptomatic bradycardia is a finding in search of a disease. The guideline agrees — asymptomatic SND is Class III: Harm for pacing.

Verify current grades at uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org — recommendations are periodically re-issued.

Escalate

When to refer / admit

🚑

Red flags → ED / admission

Send to the ED today — do not "arrange outpatient monitoring":
  • Syncope with any conduction abnormality on ECG (especially bifascicular block) — this is presumed paroxysmal complete block until disproven
  • Mobitz II, high-grade, or complete heart block on any tracing — regardless of how well they look
  • Wide-QRS bradycardia
  • HR <40 with symptoms, or any bradycardia with hypotension, chest pain, dyspnea at rest, or altered mentation
  • Alternating bundle branch block — the His-Purkinje system is failing in both branches
  • New AV block with suspected ischemia, Lyme carditis, or drug overdose
  • Bradycardia with K⁺ ≥6.5 or any ECG change of hyperkalemia
  • Pacemaker patient with syncope → suspect device failure; interrogate urgently
Refer to EP (non-urgent) for: symptomatic SND where you've excluded reversible causes; asymptomatic Mobitz II or complete block (they still need a device); chronotropic incompetence limiting the patient; unexplained syncope needing an ILR; any conduction disease in a patient with neuromuscular disease, a sarcoid diagnosis, or an LMNA/SCN5A family history.
"Mechanical fall" in an older adult is a diagnosis of exclusion. Patients with Stokes-Adams attacks have no prodrome and no memory of the event, so they reconstruct it as a trip. Ask the witness, not the patient. An unexplained fall with a facial injury (no protective reflex = they were unconscious before impact) is syncope until proven otherwise — and it earns an ECG.
🛏️ Wards — acute inpatient management
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria — concrete triggers

Admit forWhy — the reasoning, not the reflex
Mobitz II, high-grade, or third-degree AV blockThese earn a pacemaker regardless of symptoms (Class I, B-NR). The patient is walking around dependent on an escape rhythm that can stop without warning. Admit and monitor until the device is in.
Any symptomatic bradycardia — syncope, presyncope, HF symptoms, confusion attributable to the rateBy definition this meets the guideline's "symptomatic bradycardia" criterion and needs a disposition decision, not an outpatient Holter.
Wide-QRS bradycardia of any degreePresumed infranodal → unreliable escape → sudden progression to asystole.
Syncope + bifascicular block or any conduction disease61% of syncope patients with BBB/bifascicular block have a significant His-Purkinje abnormality at EPS (2018 guideline §6.2). This is paroxysmal complete block until disproven.
Alternating bundle branch blockBoth fascicles are failing. This is a hair's breadth from complete block.
Bradycardia + ischemia (chest pain, troponin rise, ECG changes)The block is a symptom of the infarct. The treatment is the cath lab, not atropine.
Drug overdose — β-blocker, CCB, digoxinThese get worse over hours as absorption continues. A stable-looking CCB overdose at hour 2 can be in shock at hour 8. Sustained-release preparations are the classic trap.
Suspected Lyme carditisBlock fluctuates by the hour and can jump from first-degree to complete without passing through the intermediate stages. Admit for telemetry while treating; most recover fully and avoid a device.
Bradycardia + K⁺ ≥6.5 or any hyperkalemic ECG changeA reversible, lethal, and fast-moving cause.
Pacemaker patient with syncope or bradycardiaDevice failure, lead problem, or exit block. Interrogate immediately — do not assume the device is working because it's there.
Who does NOT need admission: asymptomatic sinus bradycardia; the athlete with a resting rate of 42 whose rate rises on walking; asymptomatic first-degree block or Mobitz I with a narrow QRS and no symptoms; nocturnal-only bradycardia in a patient who feels fine (work up the apnea as an outpatient). The guideline is explicit for SND: "Because patients are typically stable and minimally symptomatic on presentation with SND, no acute therapy is usually required, and evaluation… can be performed in an outpatient setting."
Orders

Admission order set

🧪

Labs, monitoring, and the things people forget

Continuous telemetryNon-negotiable. You are watching for the level of block and for pauses. Ask the nurse to print a strip during any symptom — symptom-rhythm correlation is the entire diagnosis and it cannot be reconstructed later.Admit
Pacer pads ON the patientNot "at the bedside" — on the chest, connected, for any wide-QRS block, high-grade block, or complete block. When these arrest, you have seconds. Pads take 90.Admit
12-lead ECG + serial ECGsOn arrival and with any change. The level of block can migrate.Admit
BMP + Mg²⁺ + Ca²⁺STAT. Potassium first.STAT
TSHOn admission.Admit
TroponinIf any ischemic suspicion. Interpret cautiously — bradycardia alone causes demand ischemia.If suspected
Digoxin levelIf on digoxin. ≥6–8 h post-dose. Check the K⁺ alongside it.If on digoxin
Lyme serologyEndemic area, young patient, fluctuating block. Send it — but start empiric therapy on suspicion, don't wait.If suggestive
EchocardiogramWithin 24 h for new high-grade block: structural disease, EF (drives CRT vs RV lead), and — if there's fever — vegetations.<24 h
HOLD all AV nodal blocking agentsβ-blocker, diltiazem/verapamil, digoxin, amiodarone. Write it explicitly — home-med reconciliation cheerfully re-orders metoprolol on a patient in complete heart block.Admit
Atropine at the bedside1 mg, drawn up. Unless the patient is a heart transplant recipient — then it is contraindicated (Class III: Harm) and you want aminophylline instead.Admit
IV access ×2You may need drips fast.Admit
EP consultSame day for any pacemaker indication. Overnight if unstable.Admit
Write "no AV nodal agents" in the allergy/alert field, not just the med list. The most common inpatient harm event in this population is the reflexive re-ordering of a home β-blocker on a patient admitted for heart block.
Treat

Acute management

💊

The bradycardia algorithm — stepwise, with doses

The 2020 AHA Adult Bradycardia Algorithm, with the doses as the AHA prints them. Note the "and/or" between pacing and drips — that is deliberate (see the dopamine-vs-pacing trial below).
The only branch point that matters: is this bradycardia causing hypotension, altered mental status, shock, ischemic chest discomfort, or acute heart failure? If no → monitor, observe, and hunt the cause. Do not treat a number. If yes → atropine, then pacing and/or a drip. Nothing about the rate itself changes this — a comfortable patient at 38 needs a workup, not a drug; a shocked patient at 48 needs both.
1
Atropine — first-line if unstable
1 mg IV bolus · repeat q3–5 min · MAX 3 mg
▾
Atropine is a parasympatholytic — it blocks the M₂ muscarinic receptor. It does not stimulate the sinus node; it releases the vagal brake. The guideline: it "facilitates sinoatrial conduction and increases sinus node automaticity at doses of approximately 0.5 to 2 mg, with a half-life of approximately 2 hours." No vagal tone present → no effect.
SourceStartTitrationMax
2020 AHA ACLS1 mg IV bolusRepeat every 3–5 min3 mg total
2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Table 80.5–1 mg IVRepeat every 3–5 min3 mg total

The two differ only in the first dose. Both cap at 3 mg and repeat q3–5 min. Teach the ACLS 1 mg as the operational answer — 2020 raised it from 0.5 mg precisely because of the bimodal effect below.

Never give less than 0.5 mg. Verbatim from the guideline: "The sinoatrial node response to atropine is bimodal, lower doses (usually <0.5 mg) are associated with slower rates and acceleration with higher doses." A timid 0.3 mg dose slows the patient down. This is the mechanism behind ACLS's move to a flat 1 mg.
SituationDoes atropine work?What to do instead
Nodal block (narrow QRS, Mobitz I, 1°)Yes — IIa, C-LD—
Infranodal (wide QRS, Mobitz II, most CHB)No — and may worsen itDon't chase it. Pads + drip + call for a wire.
Heart transplantCONTRAINDICATED — Class III: HarmAminophylline 6 mg/kg in 100–200 mL IV over 20–30 min; or theophylline 300 mg IV. Or pace.
HypothermiaNo — the node is cold, not vagally brakedRewarm. Handle gently.
HyperkalemiaNoCalcium first, then shift and remove K⁺.
Atropine in the transplanted heart caused paradoxical heart block or sinus arrest in 20% of a 25-patient series. The denervated heart has no vagal tone to block — and parasympathetic reinnervation is uncommon (11% vs 34% for sympathetic). The Acute Bradycardia Algorithm carries the footnote in bold: "Atropine should not be given in patients after heart transplant."

Side effects to expect: dry mouth, blurred vision, anhidrosis, urinary retention, delirium (especially in the elderly — anticholinergic burden). "Excessive increase in heart rate may be problematic, particularly in patients with acute MI." Rarely provokes intra-atrial reentry or sinus pauses. Atropine is a bridge, not a plan — the guideline: "Because of its short duration of action, it is generally used as a bridge to longer-lasting therapy."

2
Transcutaneous pacing AND/OR a chronotrope drip
Both are legitimate — the trial says they're equivalent.
▾
Why "and/or" and not a hierarchy: 82 patients with unstable bradycardia refractory to fluids and atropine were randomized to transcutaneous pacing vs dopamine — and there was no difference in survival to hospital discharge or serious adverse events (2018 guideline §5.3.2.1). Use what you can deliver fastest and titrate to perfusion. In practice: pads are already on, so start pacing while the drip is mixed.

The drips — full doses from 2018 guideline Table 8

AgentReceptors / mechanismStart → Titration → MaxWhen to pick it
DopamineDose-dependent: 1–2 mcg/kg/min predominantly vasodilatory; 5–20 β₁ chronotropy + inotropy dominate; higher adds α₁ vasoconstrictionStart 5 mcg/kg/min → increase by 5 every 2 min → max 20 mcg/kg/minThe ACLS default drip. Also raises BP as you climb — useful when the bradycardia has produced hypotension.
EpinephrinePotent β₁ (rate + contractility) + β₂ + α₁ (vasoconstriction)2–10 mcg/min IV, titrate to response
or 0.1–0.5 mcg/kg/min		Bradycardia with hypotension/shock. The ACLS alternative to dopamine.
IsoproterenolNonselective β agonist — "enhancing sinus and atrioventricular nodal function without exerting a vasopressor effect"20–60 mcg IV bolus, then 10–20 mcg doses
or infusion 1–20 mcg/min		Pure chronotropy when you don't need pressure. Elicited an escape rhythm in 68% of pacemaker-dependent patients during generator change.
Dobutamineβ₁ > β₂ — inotropy + chronotropy, mild vasodilationNamed in the guideline recommendation; dose per your institution's inotrope protocol (typically 2–20 mcg/kg/min)Named alongside the others in the IIb recommendation. Useful when low output coexists.
AminophyllineNonselective adenosine receptor antagonist + PDE inhibitor — blocks the adenosine surge that mediates block in inferior MI250 mg IV bolus (inferior MI)
6 mg/kg in 100–200 mL over 20–30 min (transplant / spinal cord injury)		2°/3° block with acute inferior MI (IIb, C-LD); post-transplant; spinal cord injury
Isoproterenol is NOT in the 2020 AHA bradycardia algorithm — the official Doses/Details box lists only atropine, dopamine, and epinephrine. Its dosing comes from the 2018 guideline Table 8. And know its trap: because it "increases myocardial oxygen demand through β₁ effects while decreasing coronary perfusion attributable to β₂ effects, it is best avoided in settings where there is concern for coronary ischemia." It can also worsen hypotension through vasodilation. The whole β-agonist recommendation is conditioned on "low likelihood of coronary ischemia."

Transcutaneous pacing — how to actually do it

Pad position
AP
anterior-posterior preferred; avoids the generator if one is implanted
Rate
60–80/min
adjust to clinical response (ACLS training source — the AHA algorithm itself doesn't specify)
Output
↑ until capture
then set 10 mA above threshold; typical capture 65–100 mA
Sedation
Mandatory
it is genuinely painful — analgesia + sedation if conscious
Confirm capture mechanically, not electrically. The monitor will happily show a "paced" complex after every spike that captured nothing. Confirm with a femoral pulse or POCUS — never the carotid, because the pacer makes the pectoral and neck muscles twitch and you will feel your own stimulus artifact and call it a pulse. The guideline is blunt about the limitation: "Given the difficulty in assessing reliable myocardial capture with transcutaneous pacing, this method should only be used if other temporary methods are delayed or not available." TCP is a bridge measured in minutes-to-an-hour, not a plan.
3
Transvenous pacing → permanent device
Expert consultation + a wire.
▾

Temporary transvenous pacing is reasonable (IIa, B-NR) for 2°/3° AV block with symptoms or hemodynamic compromise refractory to medical therapy. It is a bridge to a permanent device or to recovery of a reversible cause — not a destination.

  • Access: right internal jugular or left subclavian give the most favorable, gentlest curve to the RV apex.
  • Settings: rate 60–80; find the capture threshold, then set output at 2–3× threshold for a safety margin; sensitivity ~2 mV (demand/VVI mode).
  • Complications: RV perforation → tamponade (sudden hypotension + loss of capture = get an echo now), lead dislodgement, infection, VT from lead irritation, pneumothorax.
  • If it will be needed for days: "For patients who require prolonged temporary transvenous pacing, it is reasonable to choose an externalized permanent active fixation lead over a standard passive fixation temporary pacing lead" (IIa, B-NR). This is the "temp-perm" — a screw-in lead attached to an external generator. Far more stable, lets the patient sit up and even walk, and is the right call for device infections needing weeks of antibiotics before reimplantation.
Every temporary wire is a bridge to a decision, and the decision is: is this reversible? Lyme, drug toxicity, hyperkalemia, inferior MI, and post-op vagal block often recover fully — pace them temporarily and they walk out without a device. Lev-Lenègre fibrosis, post-TAVR block, and sarcoid do not recover. Don't implant on day 1 of a reversible cause, and don't dither for a week on an irreversible one.
🧯

Cause-specific antidotes — when the rhythm is a poisoning

All doses below are verbatim from 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Table 8 unless noted. These situations are where a resident makes the biggest difference — the rhythm is a red herring; the poison is the diagnosis.

PoisoningAgentStart → TitrationWhy it works
Calcium channel blocker overdose
IIa, C-LD		10% calcium chloride1–2 g IV every 10–20 min or infusion 0.2–0.4 mL/kg/hMass-action: floods the ICaL step verapamil is blocking. CaCl₂ has 3× the elemental calcium of gluconate — central line preferred, it's a vesicant.
10% calcium gluconate3–6 g IV every 10–20 min or infusion 0.6–1.2 mL/kg/hSame mechanism; the guideline notes gluconate is used "to minimize peripheral vein irritation" — the peripheral-line choice.
β-blocker OR CCB overdose
IIa, C-LD each		Glucagon3–10 mg IV bolus → infusion 3–5 mg/hThe elegant one. Glucagon "counteracts the effects of beta blockers by activation of hepatic adenyl cyclase" — it raises cAMP bypassing the β receptor entirely, so it works even when the receptor is fully occupied by the blocker. Expect vomiting — protect the airway.
High-dose insulin (HIET)1 unit/kg IV bolus → infusion 0.5 units/kg/hThe poisoned myocardium switches from fatty-acid to carbohydrate metabolism; insulin is a direct inotrope in this state. "Follow glucose and potassium levels" — run concurrent dextrose and replace K⁺. Doses far above these are used in toxicology practice; involve your poison center.
Digoxin toxicity
IIa, C-LD		Digoxin antibody Fab (DigiFab)Dose depends on amount ingested or level. One 40-mg vial binds ≈0.5 mg of digoxin. Give over ≥30 min. May be repeated.
Formulas (external): chronic, known level → vials = (level ng/mL × kg)/100. Acute, known amount → vials = (mg ingested × 0.8)/0.5. Empiric acute, unknown → 10 vials. Empiric chronic → ~6 vials. Round up.		A monovalent antibody fragment that binds intravascular digoxin, pulling it off the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and abolishing the vagotonic drive. Clinical response in 50–90% within 30–45 min; response rates "as high as 80% to 90%… particularly in the acute setting." Adverse effects (HF, tachycardia, hypokalemia, allergy) in <10%.
Dialysis does NOT remove digoxin — Class III: No Benefit (C-LD). A systematic review of 84 patients found digoxin "is only slightly dialyzable." Its volume of distribution is enormous; it lives in tissue, not plasma. Do not put a temporary dialysis catheter in a bradycardic, coagulopathic patient for a therapy that cannot work.
Two digoxin details that change management: (1) after DigiFab, the total digoxin assay is uninterpretable — it measures antibody-bound drug. Stop sending levels and follow the patient.
