(2) Patients with hyperkalemia or arrhythmia and a digoxin level >2 mcg/L "are at increased risk of death" — in acute digoxin toxicity the potassium is the prognostic marker, and the hyperkalemia is a consequence of poisoning the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, not a separate problem.
Other reversible causeTreatmentNote
HyperkalemiaIV calcium (membrane stabilization) → insulin+dextrose, albuterol (shift) → K⁺ removal (diuresis, binders, dialysis)Calcium works in minutes and buys time; it does not lower the K⁺. Give it first when there are ECG changes.
Lyme carditisIV ceftriaxone for hospitalized/high-grade block, stepping down to oral doxycycline once conduction improves; total course typically 14–21 daysVerify the exact regimen and duration against the current IDSA/AAN/ACR Lyme guideline before prescribing. Block is usually nodal, fluctuating, and reversible — most patients recover conduction and avoid a permanent device. Bridge with a temporary wire if needed.
Myxedema / hypothyroidismIV levothyroxine (± hydrocortisone until adrenal insufficiency is excluded)Give steroid before thyroid hormone if adrenal insufficiency is possible — replacing thyroid first can precipitate adrenal crisis.
HypothermiaRewarmingAtropine-resistant. Handle gently — a cold heart fibrillates on rough movement.
Raised ICP (Cushing reflex)Treat the ICPBradycardia + hypertension + irregular respiration = a neurosurgical emergency, not a cardiac one. Never "treat" this bradycardia.
New AV block + fever + a murmur = perivalvular abscess until proven otherwise. The aortic valve annulus sits directly on top of the AV node and His bundle. An aortic root abscess burrowing out of the annulus destroys them — so a lengthening PR interval in endocarditis is a surgical trigger, not a cardiology curiosity. Get a TEE (transthoracic is not sensitive enough for an abscess) and call surgery. Pacing the block without draining the abscess treats the monitor and lets the patient die of the infection.
Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend each day

TrendTarget / what you're watching for
Telemetry review — personally, every morningDo not accept "rate was in the 50s." Scroll it. You are looking for: the level of block, longest pause, whether the block is progressing, and whether any symptom lines up with a rhythm event. Print the strips.
Symptom–rhythm correlationThe single most valuable data point of the admission. It is the "gold standard of diagnosis" per the guideline and "confers the highest likelihood of response to therapy."
Daily 12-lead ECG (while unstable)QRS width, PR interval, level of block, escape rhythm origin, new BBB.
K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺Daily while abnormal or while on insulin therapy for CCB/BB overdose (HIET consumes potassium).
Culprit drug washoutTrack time since the last dose against the drug's half-life. Metoprolol: hours. Amiodarone: weeks to months — do not conclude "irreversible" on day 3 of amiodarone washout.
Orthostatics + ambulationCan they walk without presyncope? Does the rate rise? An unchanged rate with exertion is a chronotropic red flag.
Volume & perfusionMentation, urine output, lactate if unwell.
Post-implant (if paced)CXR for lead position + pneumothorax; wound check; device interrogation; arm restriction compliance.
The daily question is not "what's the rate?" — it is "has the block changed level, and is the cause reversing?" Those two answers decide whether this patient goes home with a device or without one.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Escalation triggers — numeric

Transfer to ICU for any of:
  • SBP <90 mm Hg or MAP <65 attributable to the bradycardia
  • Bradycardia refractory to 3 mg of atropine — you have exhausted first-line therapy
  • Requirement for any chronotrope infusion (dopamine, epinephrine, isoproterenol) — a drip is an ICU therapy
  • Transcutaneous pacing in use, or a transvenous wire in place
  • Escape rate <40 with a wide QRS, or any ventricular escape you're relying on
  • Pauses >5–6 s while awake, or any pause with loss of consciousness
  • Complete heart block complicating anterior MI — this marks a large infarct and the risk is pump failure
  • Significant β-blocker/CCB/digoxin overdose — needs HIET, glucagon, or Fab with hourly titration
  • New AV block + hemodynamic instability + fever (root abscess) — surgical emergency
  • Altered mentation, lactate rising, or oliguria from hypoperfusion
  • Torsades or ventricular arrhythmia triggered by the bradycardia (bradycardia-dependent long QT)
A patient on a chronotrope drip on a med-surg floor is a system failure waiting to happen. If they need the drip, they need the unit — the drug has a 2-minute titration interval and their next event is asystole.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness — all of these:

  • Definitive plan executed: either the device is in and interrogated, or the reversible cause is corrected and the rhythm has demonstrably recovered on telemetry.
  • ≥24 h of telemetry free of high-grade block, significant pauses, and symptoms after the intervention.
  • Symptoms resolved — no syncope, presyncope, or exertional intolerance.
  • Ambulating at their baseline without presyncope, with an appropriate rate response.
  • Electrolytes normalized; culprit drugs formally stopped and documented in the discharge summary with the reason, so nobody restarts them.
  • Post-implant: CXR confirms lead position and excludes pneumothorax; wound clean; patient knows the arm restrictions.
  • Follow-up booked: device clinic ~7–14 days for a wound check; EP/cardiology; PCP.
  • Driving discussed and documented (jurisdiction-specific).
Do not discharge: a patient with untreated Mobitz II / high-grade / complete block "because they feel fine" — they meet a Class I pacing indication regardless of symptoms. Or a patient whose only "improvement" is that you stopped their metoprolol 12 hours ago and the rate came up — the block may be structural and the drug merely unmasked it. Give it a real washout and re-look.

Home

Device implanted and working, or cause reversed and rhythm stable. Independent, ambulating, understands restrictions. The large majority.

Home health

Needs wound care, INR checks, or a nurse visit; lives alone; borderline mobility after a syncopal fall.

SNF

Deconditioned after a prolonged admission or a fall-related injury. Needs 24-h skilled nursing, <3 h therapy/day.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Uncommon here — reserved for a significant injury from a syncopal fall (hip fracture, TBI) with ≥3 h therapy/day across ≥2 disciplines.

LTAC

Rare. Prolonged complex care — e.g. a device infection needing weeks of IV antibiotics on a temp-perm wire, or vent weaning after a complicated course.

Hospice / palliative

Every device recommendation is conditioned on "meaningful survival of >1 year expected." If it isn't, a pacemaker is a procedure without a benefit. Bradycardia can be a comfortable way to die — say so, kindly, and honestly.
Post-implant patient instructions people forget to give: no lifting the arm above shoulder height and nothing heavy for ~4–6 weeks (lead dislodgement is a first-month problem); keep the wound dry; watch for fever, swelling, or redness; carry the device card; MRI is fine with modern MR-conditional systems but must be run under a device protocol; avoid arc welding and leaning over a running alternator; phones/headphones in the shirt pocket over the device are a real (if minor) magnet issue. And tell them what to expect: they may feel better within a day.
🫀 ICU — critical care, pacing & the peri-procedural conduction disasters
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

When it belongs in the unit

Bradycardia earns an ICU bed for one of three reasons: the rhythm is not perfusing, the therapy needs a unit (drip, wire, pads), or the cause is a poisoning that will get worse before it gets better.

TriggerThreshold
Hemodynamic failureSBP <90 / MAP <65 attributable to the rate; lactate rising; oliguria; altered mentation
Refractory to first-linePersisting after 3 mg atropine
Any chronotrope infusionDopamine, epinephrine, isoproterenol — the titration interval is 2 minutes
Pacing in useTranscutaneous pacing running, or a transvenous wire in place (a wire is an ICU device: it dislodges, it perforates)
Unreliable escapeWide-QRS escape <40, or complete block with a ventricular escape
ToxicologicSignificant β-blocker / CCB / digoxin overdose needing HIET, glucagon, or Fab
Bradycardia-triggered VTTorsades from a bradycardia-dependent long QT — needs overdrive pacing, not amiodarone
Post-arrestBradyasystolic arrest with ROSC
Structural emergencyNew AV block + fever (root abscess); anterior MI + CHB
Bradycardia can kill through tachycardia. A slow rate lengthens the QT; a long QT invites torsades de pointes (pause-dependent, "bradycardia-dependent" TdP). The treatment is magnesium and rate acceleration — isoproterenol or overdrive pacing to ~90–100 — not an antiarrhythmic. Giving amiodarone here makes it worse: you'd be lengthening the QT of a patient whose problem is a long QT. If a bradycardic patient has polymorphic VT, the answer is to speed them up.
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, leads, and what to trend

ItemWhy here specifically
Arterial lineThe most useful line in this diagnosis. During transcutaneous pacing the monitor shows a QRS after every spike whether or not the heart contracted — the arterial waveform is the only thing that tells you a beat actually ejected. One arterial upstroke per pacing spike = capture. It also gives beat-to-beat MAP while you titrate.
Central accessRoute for the transvenous wire (RIJ or left subclavian) and for chronotrope drips. Get it early — placing a central line in a peri-arrest bradycardic patient is a bad time.
Pacer pads, connectedOn the chest, machine on, in demand mode, threshold pre-tested if the patient can tolerate it.
Continuous 12-lead-capable telemetryYou need to see the level of block change, not just the rate.
Trend: escape rate & QRS widthA widening escape or a falling escape rate = the backup pacemaker is failing. That's the pre-arrest sign.
Trend: K⁺, Mg²⁺, glucoseHourly glucose + K⁺ on HIET. It consumes both.
Trend: lactate, urine output, mentationIs the rate perfusing? That is the only question the number can't answer.
Pseudo-bradycardia is real. The guideline warns to "correlate slow radial pulses with precordial auscultation or carotid pulse assessment, as some rhythms (e.g., ventricular or conducted atrial bigeminy) can be misinterpreted as bradycardia if premature beats generate inadequate stroke volume to be palpable peripherally." A patient in bigeminy at 80 has a radial pulse of 40. Listen to the heart before you push atropine at a pulse you counted at the wrist.
Support

Chronotropes & pressors

💉

Which drip, why, and the dose

Every drip below is an attempt to do one of two things: put cAMP back into a sinus nodal cell (to steepen phase 4) or put calcium through ICaL (to make the AV node conduct). The receptor you choose decides whether you also get contractility and vasoconstriction — which is how you match the drug to the failure.
AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeHemodynamic effectWhen to pick
DopamineDose-dependent: 1–2 mcg/kg/min dopaminergic/vasodilatory; 5–20 β₁ chronotropy + inotropy; higher = α₁5 → +5 q2min → 20 mcg/kg/min↑HR, ↑CO, ↑SVR at higher dosesThe ACLS default. Bradycardia with hypotension. >20 mcg/kg/min "may result in vasoconstriction or arrhythmias."
Epinephrineβ₁ (rate, inotropy) + β₂ (vasodilation) + α₁ (vasoconstriction)2–10 mcg/min or 0.1–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑↑HR, ↑↑CO, ↑SVRBradycardia with shock. The most reliable rescue when you need rate and pressure.
IsoproterenolPure nonselective β (β₁+β₂), no α at all20–60 mcg IV bolus, then 10–20 mcg
or 1–20 mcg/min infusion		↑↑HR, ↑CO, ↓SVR (β₂ vasodilation)Pure chronotropy without pressure. Avoid if coronary ischemia is a concern — ↑MVO₂ via β₁ while ↓coronary perfusion via β₂. Can worsen hypotension.
Dobutamineβ₁ > β₂Per institutional protocol (typically 2–20 mcg/kg/min)↑CO, ↑HR, mild ↓SVRNamed in the guideline's IIb rec. Useful when low output coexists.
Norepinephrineα₁ ≫ β₁0.01–0.5+ mcg/kg/min↑↑SVR, mild ↑CO, little rate effectNot a chronotrope. Its place here is bradycardia + vasoplegia (e.g. septic patient who is also blocked), or to hold the MAP while pacing does the rate.
GlucagonNon-β receptor → activates hepatic adenylyl cyclase → ↑cAMP3–10 mg IV → 3–5 mg/h↑HR, ↑contractilityβ-blocker or CCB overdose. The one agent that raises cAMP with the β receptor fully blocked. Expect vomiting.
High-dose insulin (HIET)Direct inotrope in the poisoned myocardium (shifts it to carbohydrate metabolism)1 unit/kg bolus → 0.5 units/kg/h (guideline); toxicology practice escalates well beyond this↑contractility, ↑COβ-blocker/CCB overdose (IIa). "Follow glucose and potassium levels" — run dextrose, replace K⁺.
CalciumMass action on the blocked ICaLCaCl₂ 1–2 g q10–20min (or 0.2–0.4 mL/kg/h); Ca-gluconate 3–6 g q10–20min (or 0.6–1.2 mL/kg/h)↑contractility, ↑ AV conductionCCB overdose; hyperkalemia (membrane stabilization).
Aminophylline / theophyllineAdenosine receptor antagonist + PDE inhibitorInferior MI: 250 mg IV bolus
Transplant/SCI: 6 mg/kg over 20–30 min		↑HRInferior MI block (IIb) · post-transplant (IIa) · spinal cord injury (IIa) — the three places atropine won't serve you.
Match the drug to the failure. Rate problem only, no ischemia → isoproterenol or dopamine. Rate + pressure problem → epinephrine. Pressure problem with an adequate rate → norepinephrine. β-blocker on board → glucagon (bypasses the blocked receptor). CCB on board → calcium + HIET. Denervated heart → aminophylline. Inferior MI → aminophylline (blocks the adenosine surge). No response to any of it → the answer was always pacing.
The evidence base here is thinner than the confident tables suggest. Isoproterenol: "there are no clinical trials or observational series data to support or discourage its use" in sinus bradycardia, and two RCTs in cardiac arrest showed no ROSC or survival benefit. Aminophylline for inferior-MI block rests on "several small case series of up to 8 patients," and a large RCT showed no benefit in out-of-hospital bradyasystolic arrest. These are IIa/IIb recommendations for a reason — treat them as reasonable attempts while you arrange the definitive therapy.
Pacing

Temporary pacing — the procedural core

⚡

Transcutaneous → transvenous → temp-perm

Transvenous pacing — settings

Access
RIJ / L subclavian
gentlest curve to the RV apex
Mode
VVI (demand)
so it doesn't compete with intrinsic beats
Rate
60–80/min
titrate to perfusion
Output
2–3× threshold
find threshold, then set the safety margin
Sensitivity
~2 mV
must sense intrinsic beats to stay in demand
Threshold check
Daily
rising threshold = lead moving or tissue reacting
The complications that kill: RV perforation → tamponade (sudden hypotension + loss of capture + rising JVP → echo now, this is the one that gets missed); lead dislodgement (loss of capture — the most common failure); infection (rises steeply after ~48 h); VT from lead irritation; pneumothorax from the access. Every one of these presents as "the pacer stopped working" — so every loss of capture deserves a CXR and an echo, not just a knob turn.
If pacing will be needed for more than a couple of days, ask for a "temp-perm." The guideline (IIa, B-NR): "For patients who require prolonged temporary transvenous pacing, it is reasonable to choose an externalized permanent active fixation lead over a standard passive fixation temporary pacing lead." A screw-in lead tunnelled and attached to an external generator is dramatically more stable, lets the patient sit up and mobilize, and is the right answer when you need weeks — classically a device infection that has to be extracted and antibiotic-treated before reimplantation.
The guideline's honest verdict on both techniquesOn transcutaneous: "Transcutaneous pacing, devised >60 years ago, has a limited role in the acute treatment of atrioventricular block because of the painful nature of the stimulation and difficulty in ascertaining reliable myocardial capture" — and it "should only be used if other temporary methods are delayed or not available." On transvenous: these techniques "have been used for nearly 60 years but have remarkably little data to guide their appropriate use." Both are bridges built on tradition rather than trials. Know their failure modes, and get to the definitive answer quickly.
Airway

Airway & the peri-intubation trap

🌬️

Intubating the bradycardic patient

Bradycardia is not a lung disease, so there is no ARDSnet table here. But intubating a bradycardic patient is one of the most dangerous things you will do, and it is a predictable danger:

The threatWhyWhat to do
Vagal surge on laryngoscopyDirect stimulation of the posterior pharynx → massive parasympathetic outflow onto an already-braked nodeHave atropine drawn up and pads on before you touch the airway. Consider pre-treating.
HypoxiaHypoxia itself is a potent bradycardic stimulus — and this patient has no rate reservePre-oxygenate hard. Apneic oxygenation. Do not accept a long apneic period.
PropofolVasodilation + negative inotropy + direct bradycardia — it hits the same patient from three directionsUse ketamine (preserves sympathetic tone) or etomidate (hemodynamically neutral). Avoid propofol.
SuccinylcholineRaises K⁺ by ~0.5–1.0 mEq/L; and it is itself a muscarinic agonist at the SA node → bradycardia, especially with repeat dosingAvoid if hyperkalemia is the cause of the block. Use rocuronium. (Succinylcholine-induced bradycardia is a classic in children and with second doses.)
Positive pressure↓preload in a patient whose output is already rate-limitedGentle tidal volumes; expect the BP to fall; have the pressor running before you push the drugs.
Dexmedetomidine for post-tube sedationα₂ agonist → the exact mechanism that causes bradycardiaPick a different sedative in a blocked patient.
The rule: resuscitate before you intubate, and pace before you sedate. For a patient in high-grade block who needs an airway, get the pads on and capture established (or the wire in) first. Intubation is a vagal, hypoxic, hypotensive insult delivered to a heart with no reserve — the peri-intubation arrest in this population is bradyasystolic and it is preventable.
Special

Peri-procedural & special situations

⚙️

Post-TAVR, post-surgical, post-MI, post-transplant

Post-TAVR conduction disease — the modern bread-and-butter

The aortic annulus sits directly on the His bundle and left bundle. Expanding a metal frame inside it injures them mechanically. New LBBB and high-grade block are expected complications, not surprises — and the block can be delayed, which is why the monitoring question matters.

TAVR: the valve frame is deployed within the native annulus — millimetres from the His bundle and left bundle branch. The conduction system is collateral damage of a mechanical problem.
Image: Dr. Ofir Koren MD FACC FESC, CC BY-SA 2.0 — Wikimedia Commons
The destination for many of them: a permanent pacemaker. Trace the leads on every post-implant film — generator in the left pre-pectoral pocket, lead through subclavian → SVC → RA, second lead across the tricuspid to the RV apex. Check for pneumothorax while you're there.
Image: Sunzi99, CC BY 3.0 — Wikimedia Commons
ClassLevelRecommendationSource
IB-NRNew AV block after TAVR with symptoms or hemodynamic instability that does not resolve → permanent pacing before discharge2018 ACC/AHA
IBComplete or high-degree AV block persisting 24–48 h after TAVI → permanent pacing2021 ESC
ICNew-onset alternating BBB after TAVI → permanent pacing2021 ESC
IIaBPre-existing RBBB + any further conduction disturbance during/after TAVI → early permanent pacing2021 ESC
IIaB-NRNew persistent BBB after TAVR → careful surveillance for bradycardia2018 ACC/AHA
IIaCNew LBBB with QRS >150 ms or PR >240 ms with no further prolongation over >48 h → ambulatory monitoring (7–30 d) or EPS2021 ESC
IIbB-NRNew persistent LBBB after TAVR → PPM may be considered2018 ACC/AHA
IIICProphylactic PPM before TAVI is NOT indicated in patients with RBBB and no pacing indication2021 ESC
Pre-existing RBBB is the single biggest risk factor for needing a pacemaker after TAVR — and the mechanism is elegant: the patient is already living on their left bundle, and TAVR is a procedure that injures the left bundle. Take out the left and they have nothing. That's why "RBBB + any new conduction change post-TAVI" jumps straight to early pacing (IIa, B) while everyone else gets watched. ESC flags the high-risk trio for new-LBBB patients: AF, prolonged PR, and LVEF <40%. Post-TAVR, an HV ≥65 ms was modestly predictive of high-grade block (sensitivity 80%, specificity 79%).

Post-cardiac-surgery & post-septal-reduction

  • Surgical AVR / MVR / TVR: new SND or AV block "associated with persistent symptoms or hemodynamic instability that does not resolve" → permanent pacing before discharge (I, B-NR). Routine temporary epicardial wires at surgery (I / IIa depending on valve). For tricuspid surgery at high risk of block, place permanent epicardial leads intraoperatively (IIa, C-LD) — a transvenous lead across a new tricuspid prosthesis is a problem you don't want.
  • ESC observation window: "A period of clinical observation for at least 5 days is indicated" after cardiac surgery — "however, in the case of complete AVB with low or no escape rhythm when resolution is unlikely, this observation period can be shortened."
  • Alcohol septal ablation / surgical myectomy: Mobitz II, high-grade, or persistent complete block afterwards → PPM before discharge (I, B-NR). Septal ablation deliberately infarcts the septum — where the conduction system lives. RBBB after alcohol septal ablation, LBBB after myectomy.

Post-MI — and why "5 days" is an ESC number

SocietyWhat it actually says
2018 ACC/AHAI, B-NR: patients with SND or AV block after acute MI "should undergo a waiting period before determining the need for permanent pacing" — no number in the recommendation. The only figure is supportive text: "the clinician should carefully consider and generally avoid early permanent pacing (<72 hours)."
2021 ESCClass I, Level C: "Implantation of a permanent pacemaker is indicated… when AVB does not resolve within a waiting period of at least 5 days after MI." Supportive text allows 5–10 days, individualized — shortened for unsuccessful/late revascularization, anterior MI, bifascicular block, or progression of block.
Two Class III: Harm recommendations after MI (both B-NR): do not implant a permanent pacemaker for transient AV block that resolves, and do not implant for a new bundle branch block or isolated fascicular block in the absence of 2°/3° block. The guideline's reasoning is worth internalizing: "Temporary pacing does not by itself constitute an indication for permanent pacing," and PPM complications "including death range from 3% to 7%." An unnecessary device is not a free hedge.
The prognosis after anterior MI with complete block is not about the block. The guideline: "the long-term prognosis… is related primarily to the extent of myocardial injury… rather than the atrioventricular block itself," and "regardless of whether the infarction is anterior or inferior, the development of an intraventricular conduction delay reflects extensive myocardial damage rather than an electrical problem in isolation." The data bear it out: CHB complicates only ~1.7% of anterior STEMIs (vs ~10.7% of non-anterior) — it is rare but marks a huge infarct, and the terminal event is cardiogenic shock, not asystole. Pacing corrects the rhythm and does not touch the reason they're dying.

Post-transplant & spinal cord injury

  • Heart transplant: denervated → atropine is Class III: Harm (paradoxical block or sinus arrest in 20%). Use aminophylline 6 mg/kg IV over 20–30 min or theophylline 300 mg IV → 5–10 mg/kg/d PO (IIa, C-LD). ESC: observe up to 6 weeks before implanting (IIa, C); pace for chronotropic incompetence persisting >6 weeks (IIa, C).
  • Acute spinal cord injury: loss of sympathetic outflow above T6 leaves the vagus unopposed → profound, recurrent bradycardia, classically on tracheal suctioning (a vagal stimulus with no sympathetic counterbalance). Aminophylline or theophylline is reasonable (IIa, C-LD). Note the guideline's own caveat: effective doses here "often result in serum levels below the usual effective range."

Refractory / rescue

If a patient is capturing and still dying, the bradycardia was not the problem — look for the cause you missed (massive overdose, tamponade from your own wire, hyperkalemia, cardiogenic shock from the infarct). VA-ECMO is a last resort for refractory toxicologic cardiogenic shock (massive CCB/β-blocker overdose is one of the few genuinely reversible ECMO indications — the poison clears and the myocardium recovers). Get the poison center involved early; their HIET doses go far above the guideline table.

Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Downgrade when ALL of these are true:
  • Off all chronotrope infusions ≥6–12 h with a stable rate
  • No transcutaneous pacing, and the transvenous wire is out — or the permanent device is implanted and interrogated
  • Perfusing rhythm: SBP >90 / MAP >65 without support; lactate normalized; mentation and urine output at baseline
  • No high-grade block or significant pauses on the last ≥24 h of telemetry
  • The cause is addressed — K⁺ corrected, drug cleared or antidote complete, apnea treated, artery opened
  • Toxicology: off HIET/glucagon with stable glucose and K⁺, and past the peak absorption window for a sustained-release ingestion
Not yet if…
  • They still have a temporary wire — a wire is an ICU device. It dislodges and perforates, and the floor cannot rescue that.
  • They are pacemaker-dependent on a temporary system awaiting a permanent device. There is no escape rhythm underneath. One dislodgement = asystole.
  • The bradycardia is drug-induced by an agent that hasn't cleared — a "fixed" rate at hour 6 of an amiodarone or sustained-release diltiazem problem is a rate that can relapse at hour 20.
  • Digoxin toxicity where you gave Fab but the volume of distribution is still redistributing — rebound toxicity is real in chronic poisoning. And you cannot follow levels anymore.
  • The escape rhythm is wide and <40, even if the BP is currently fine. That is a rhythm waiting to stop.
  • New AV block + endocarditis until the TEE has excluded a root abscess and surgery has weighed in.
  • Anterior MI + CHB with any shock physiology — the block is the least of it.
ICU disposition & goals of careMost of these patients get a device and go home. But two conversations belong here. First: every pacing recommendation in the guideline is conditioned on "meaningful survival of greater than 1 year is expected" — for a frail, dying patient, bradycardia is often a comfortable terminal rhythm, and implanting a device is a procedure without a benefit. Second, and the guideline is unusually direct about it (Top-10 Message #9): "Using the principles of shared decision-making and informed consent/refusal, [a patient] with decision-making capacity or his/her legally defined surrogate has the right to refuse or request withdrawal of pacemaker therapy, even if the patient is pacemaker dependent, which should be considered palliative, end-of-life care, and not physician-assisted suicide." Deactivating a pacemaker in a dying, pacemaker-dependent patient is ethically and legally permissible. It is not something to discover for the first time at 3 a.m.
Pearls

Practice-changing pearls

💡

The fourteen things that actually change what you do

  1. "There is no established minimum heart rate below which treatment is indicated." Verbatim from the guideline. Stop asking "what's the rate?" and start asking "are the symptoms caused by the rhythm?" Symptom–rhythm correlation is the gold standard of diagnosis and the best predictor of response to pacing.
  2. Missing P waves = sinus node dysfunction. Blocked P waves = AV block. One glance sorts the entire topic.
  3. The QRS width tells you the prognosis, not the heart rate. Narrow = nodal = a reliable junctional escape at 40–60 = usually watch. Wide = infranodal = an unreliable ventricular escape at 20–40 = pads on, wire ready.
  4. Check the potassium before you page EP. Hyperkalemia is functionally a sodium-channel blocker on infranodal tissue and it is free to fix. But don't trust the tracing: ECG sensitivity for hyperkalemia is only ~34–43% — a normal-looking ECG does not exclude a lethal potassium.
  5. 2:1 block is neither Mobitz I nor Mobitz II — with one PR before each blocked P you cannot show whether it was lengthening. Mobitz II's definition formally excludes it. It is "a commonly overdiagnosed and misinterpreted arrhythmia," and calling 2:1 "Mobitz II" commits a patient to a device. Find two consecutive conducted beats, or use exercise/atropine/CSM to localize.
  6. Never give less than 0.5 mg of atropine. The SA node response is bimodal — doses <0.5 mg slow the heart. That's why 2020 ACLS moved to a flat 1 mg first dose.
  7. Atropine is contraindicated after heart transplant (Class III: Harm). It caused paradoxical heart block or sinus arrest in 20% of transplant recipients. There is no vagal brake to release in a denervated heart. Use aminophylline.
  8. Wide-QRS block + no atropine response → stop pushing atropine. The block is structural, so atropine has nothing to reverse; and because infranodal block is rate-dependent, speeding the atria drives more impulses into refractory tissue and deepens the block. A documented case: 600 mcg of atropine in 2:1 block → ventricular standstill.
  9. Vagal maneuvers improve infranodal block. Counterintuitive, useful, and it's the proof the mechanism is rate rather than receptors — carotid massage slows the atria and gives the sick His time to recover. If a maneuver that should hurt helps, you've localized the lesion.
  10. Young patient with unexplained high-grade AV block → think sarcoid, Lyme, myotonic dystrophy, LMNA. The 2014 HRS sarcoid statement: screen everyone <60 years presenting with high-degree block. Getting this right changes the device from a pacemaker to an ICD and adds immunosuppression or antibiotics.
  11. New AV block in endocarditis = perivalvular abscess until proven otherwise. The aortic annulus sits on the AV node and His. A lengthening PR is a surgical trigger. Get a TEE — not a TTE — and call surgery.
  12. Treat the apnea before you implant the box. CPAP cuts profound bradycardia, pauses and AV block by 72–89%; 86% stayed symptom-free without a pacemaker at 22 months. The guideline: treating the apnea "eliminates the need for pacemaker implantation in most patients."
  13. Wenckebach at night in a fit young athlete is normal. So are sinus bradycardia to ≥30 bpm, PR 200–400 ms, and junctional escape. Pacing physiologic vagal bradycardia is Class III: Harm. The guideline itself notes pauses >5 s are "common" during sleep. Confirm the rate rises with exertion and reassure.
  14. The pacemaker sometimes exists to let you give the β-blocker. Symptomatic block caused by necessary guideline-directed therapy is a Class I pacing indication. And if they've been on a stable dose for years (IIa, B-NR), you can skip the washout entirely — the drug didn't change, the conduction system did.
The two-sentence summary of the whole topic. In sinus node dysfunction, symptoms are everything — no symptoms, no pacemaker, and pacing helps quality of life, not survival. In infranodal AV block, symptoms are irrelevant — you pace regardless, because the escape rhythm they're living on is unreliable and the first symptom can be the last one.

Sources, trials & media

Anchor guidelines

  • 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay — Kusumoto FM, et al. Circulation 2019;140(8):e382–e482 · Heart Rhythm 2019;16:e128–e226 · JACC 2019;74:e51–e156. Circulation · Full text PDF (HRS) · PubMed. The anchor for nearly every COR/LOE, definition, and dose in this guide.
  • 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronization therapy — Glikson M, et al. Eur Heart J 2021;42(35):3427–3520. EHJ · PubMed. Still the current ESC pacing guideline as of 2026 — the 2025 CSP document is a Clinical Consensus Statement, not a guideline.
  • 2020 AHA Adult Bradycardia Algorithm (ACLS) — Official algorithm PDF · AHA algorithms index. Source of the atropine 1 mg / dopamine 5–20 / epinephrine 2–10 doses. Note: isoproterenol is NOT in this algorithm.
  • 2023 HRS/APHRS/LAHRS guideline on cardiac physiologic pacing for the avoidance and mitigation of heart failure — Chung MK, et al. Heart Rhythm 2023;20(9):e17–e91. PMC
  • 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Syncope — Shen WK, et al. ACC Ten Points
  • 2014 HRS Expert Consensus Statement on Arrhythmias Associated with Cardiac Sarcoidosis — Birnie DH, et al. Heart Rhythm 2014;11:1305–1323. Heart Rhythm. Source of the "screen all <60 y with high-degree AV block for cardiac sarcoidosis" recommendation — not the bradycardia guideline.
  • International Recommendations for ECG Interpretation in Athletes — Sharma S, et al. JACC 2017;69:1057–75. JACC. Source of the ≥30 bpm / PR 200–400 ms athlete normals.
  • USPSTF — Hypertension (A) · Statins (B) · Falls prevention (B) · AAA (B) · Screening ECG (D / I) · AF screening with ECG (I)

Key trials & landmark evidence

Trial / studyYearResultWhy it matters
MOST2002DDDR vs VVIR in SND (n=2,010): no difference in death/stroke, but DDDR reduced AF and heart failure signs and improved QOL. Post hoc: RV pacing >40% associated with ↑HF hospitalization and AF.Established dual-chamber over VVI in SND — and gave us the 40% pacing threshold that still drives the CRT-vs-RV decision.
CTOPP2000Physiologic (dual-chamber/atrial) vs ventricular pacing: no significant reduction in stroke or CV death; modest ↓ AF.The first big blow to the assumption that physiologic pacing saves lives. It improves rhythm outcomes, not mortality.
DANPACE2011AAIR vs DDDR in SND (n=1,415): no survival difference; AAIR had MORE paroxysmal AF and more reoperations.Killed single-lead atrial pacing. This is why you don't see AAI in practice despite its theoretical elegance.
UKPACE2005Dual-chamber vs single-chamber ventricular pacing in elderly patients with AV block (n=2,021): no difference in mortality.In the elderly with AV block, a simple VVI is defensible. Supports the guideline's "single chamber ventricular pacing is effective" when comorbidities dominate (I, A).
DAVID2002In ICD patients with LV dysfunction and no pacing indication, DDDR-70 was WORSE than backup VVI-40 — more death and HF hospitalization.The landmark proof that unnecessary RV pacing causes harm. The origin of "minimize ventricular pacing" as a design goal.
MVP / SAVE PACe2007Managed ventricular pacing / dual-chamber minimal ventricular pacing reduced RV pacing burden and reduced persistent AF vs conventional DDDR.Turned "minimize RV pacing" from a principle into a programmable algorithm.
BLOCK-HF2013n=691, AV block + LVEF ≤50% (mean 42.9%), 37 mo: biventricular pacing beat RV pacing on death / HF urgent care / ≥15% ↑LV end-systolic volume index.The LVEF half of the "don't just put in an RV lead" rule. Combined with MOST's 40%, it produces the modern CRT/CSP recommendation.
ISSUE-32012Reflex syncope with ILR-documented asystole, age >40: dual-chamber pacing cut 2-y syncope recurrence from 57% → 25%.Established that you pace reflex syncope only when you have documented asystole — the ILR earns the pacemaker.
BIOSync CLS2021Tilt-positive cardioinhibitory reflex syncope: pacing with closed-loop stimulation reduced syncope recurrence (16% vs 53%).Extended the pacing evidence to tilt-documented asystolic syncope — now an ESC Class I (A) indication alongside ISSUE-3.
THEOPACE1997Symptomatic SND randomized to no treatment vs oral theophylline vs pacing: theophylline raised the resting rate, but pacing was superior for symptom control.The entire evidentiary basis for theophylline's Class IIb — and the reason the definitive therapy for bradycardia is a device, not a drug.
Groh — DM1 sudden death2008n=406 myotonic dystrophy type 1: a "severe ECG abnormality" independently predicted sudden death, RR 3.30 (1.24–8.78). 27 sudden deaths.Why neuromuscular disease has the lowest pacing threshold in the guideline (Class I at HV ≥70 ms regardless of symptoms).
Wahbi — DM1 invasive strategy2012n=914 DM1: EPS + prophylactic pacing vs not. Unadjusted mortality HR 0.74 (P=.19, NS); propensity-adjusted 0.47–0.61; sudden death HR 0.24–0.28.Supports the aggressive DM1 approach — but honestly: the all-cause mortality benefit only appeared after adjustment. The sudden-death signal is the strong one. Observational, not randomized.
Jensen — SSS incidence (ARIC+CHS)2014n=20,572, ~17 y: incidence 0.8/1,000 person-years; HR 1.73 per 5-y age increment; Blacks 41% lower risk.The best population epidemiology for sick sinus syndrome. SND is a disease of aging.
Canadian Syncope Risk Score validation2020n=3,819, AUC 0.91, calibration slope 1.0. 30-d serious outcome by tier: 0.2% → 51.3%.The best-validated syncope disposition tool — implemented live in the Clinic panel.
Milanesi — HCN4 familial bradycardia2006An HCN4 mutation near the cAMP-binding site caused familial sinus bradycardia; mutant channels activate at more negative voltages, changes that "mimic those of mild vagal stimulation."Proof that the funny current sets the human resting heart rate — the mechanism of this guide made molecular.
Baruscotti — HCN4 knockout2011Adult cardiac HCN4 ablation: If ↓~70%, severe bradycardia, and progressive AV block (1° → 2:1 → complete).One channel produces both halves of this guide — SND and heart block.
Pro@Heart — elite athlete Holter2026n=465 elite endurance athletes: 38% had min HR ≤40; pauses ≥3 s in only 3%; longest an asymptomatic nocturnal 5.4 s pause; no correlation with adverse outcomes over 5.5 y.The modern dataset for what is actually normal in an athlete's night — and reassurance that it doesn't predict harm.

Deliberate omissions — things this guide does NOT claimSeveral widely-repeated "facts" were checked against the primary sources during this build and could not be verified, so they are absent by design rather than by oversight: the ">50 mmHg systolic drop" criterion for carotid sinus hypersensitivity (absent from both the 2018 ACC/AHA and 2021 ESC texts); the claim that the 2018 guideline discourages the term "trifascicular block" (it does not — it uses the term in a Class IIb recommendation); a ">3 s pause while awake = pathologic" rule (the guideline uses >3 s only to define a sinus pause and explicitly states it "should not be used for the diagnosis of SND" alone); specific HRS remote-monitoring intervals; and any giant-cell myocarditis pacing class (no such recommendation exists in either guideline). Where a number could not be traced to a primary source, this guide says so instead of printing it.

Educational reference for an incoming IM resident. Verify every dose against your institution's formulary and the current guideline before acting on any individual patient. Class-of-recommendation and level-of-evidence labels are quoted from the 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS bradycardia guideline and the 2021 ESC pacing guideline as attributed; ACLS doses are from the 2020 AHA Adult Bradycardia Algorithm. Where the two societies differ, both are shown rather than blended.
